leads.text:
[Cite as U.S. Bank Trust Natl. Assn. v. He, 2026-Ohio-4121.] 

IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF OHIO 

TENTH APPELLATE DISTRICT 

U.S. Bank Trust National Association, : 

 Plaintiff-Appellee, : No. 26AP-359 
 (C.P.C. No. 24CV-1046) 
v. : 
 (REGULAR CALENDAR) 
Xiaowei He, : 

 Defendant-Appellant. : 

D E C I S I O N 

Rendered on October 20, 2026 

On brief: Robertson, Anschutz, Schneid, Crane & Partners, 
PLLC, and Brian S. Jackson, for appellee. Argued: Brian S. 
Jackson. 

On brief: Xiaowei He, pro se. Argued: Xiaowei He. 

APPEAL from the Franklin County Court of Common Pleas 

EDELSTEIN, J. 
{¶ 1} Defendant-appellant, Xiaowei He, appeals from a judgment entry and decree 
of foreclosure of the Franklin County Court of Common Pleas entered in favor of plaintiff-
appellee, U.S. Bank Trust National Association (“U.S. Bank”). For the following reasons, 
we affirm. 
I. Facts and Procedural History 
{¶ 2} This matter involves a foreclosure action for the real property located at 5027 
Hibbs Drive in Columbus, Ohio (“property”). On March 25, 2013, Ms. He executed a 
promissory note in favor of Fifth Third Mortgage Company secured by a mortgage on the 
No. 26AP-359 2 

property. (Compl. Ex. A, B.) On February 6, 2024, Fifth Third Bank, National Association 
fka Fifth Third Bank Successor by Merger to Fifth Third Mortgage Company (“Fifth Third”) 
filed a complaint in foreclosure against Ms. He and her unknown spouse alleging Ms. He 
defaulted on the note and mortgage. Ms. He filed a motion for an extension of time to 
respond, and the trial court granted her leave to file an answer within 28 days of April 17, 
2024. 
{¶ 3} On August 1, 2024, well after Ms. He failed to answer within the extended 
time, Fifth Third filed a motion for default judgment. Subsequently, on September 13, 
2024, Fifth Third filed a motion to stay pending loss mitigation. The trial court granted the 
motion to stay on October 7, 2024. 
{¶ 4} On February 3, 2025, the trial court substituted Select Portfolio Servicing, 
Inc. as the plaintiff. The trial court reactivated the case on June 29, 2025 and advised that 
it would set the pending motion for default judgment for a ruling.1 The trial court issued a 
second substitution order on September 15, 2025, this time substituting U.S. Bank as owner 
trustee for RCAF Acquisition Trust as the plaintiff. 
{¶ 5} On December 15, 2025, U.S. Bank filed a motion for summary judgment. U.S. 
Bank argued Ms. He defaulted on the note and mortgage by failing to make the payment 
due December 1, 2022 and all subsequent months . To support its motion for summary 
judgment, U.S. Bank filed an affidavit of Nik Fox, a corporate appearance representative of 
the loan servicer, authenticating the promissory note, the mortgage, and the loan payment 
history. Ms. He filed a memorandum in opposition to the motion for summary judgment 
asserting there existed “a fully executed and notarized Loan Modification Agreement dated 
August 1, 2024” which “materially altered [Ms. He’s] payment obligations and [U.S. Bank’s] 
contractual right to accelerate.” (Memo in Opp. at 1-2.) Ms. He filed her own affidavit, a 
timeline of her communications with the loan servicers, and five pages of a document she 
described as the “[r]elevant [p]ages of [the] Loan Modification Agreement.” (Id. at 5.) 
{¶ 6} In a March 20, 2026 decision and entry, the trial court granted U.S. Bank’s 
motion for summary judgment. The trial court considered the Civ.R. 56 evidentiary 
materials submitted by U.S. Bank and concluded it is the holder of the note secured by the 

1 The court did not rule on that motion for default judgment. 
No. 26AP-359 3 

mortgage, Ms. He is in default, all conditions precedent have been met, and U.S. Bank 
established the amount of principal and interest due. Additionally, the trial court found 
that although Ms. He referenced a Loan Modification Agreement, she did not provide any 
evidentiary materials demonstrating U.S. Bank or its predecessors executed the agreement, 
the loan servicer implemented the agreement, or the terms of the agreement actually 
altered U.S. Bank’s contractual right to enforce the note and mortgage. The trial court then 
entered a judgment entry and decree of foreclosure on April 7, 2026. Ms. He timely appeals. 
II. Assignments of Error 
{¶ 7} Ms. He raises the following three assignments of error for our review: 
[I.] The trial court erred in granting summary judgment where 
genuine issues of material fact existed. 

[II.] The trial court erred in failing to properly consider 
evidence demonstrating the existence and handling of a signed 
and notarized loan modification agreement. 

[III.] The trial court erred in granting summary judgment 
where the arrears calculation was inconsistent with the 
acknowledged loan modification. 

III. Standard of Review 
{¶ 8} An appellate court reviews a trial court’s grant of summary judgment under 
a de novo standard. Estate of Sample v. Xenos Christian Fellowship, Inc. , 2021-Ohio-
3898, ¶ 9 (10th Dist.). “[D]e novo appellate review means that the court of appeals 
independently reviews the record and affords no deference to the trial court’s decision.” 
(Internal quotations and citations omitted.) Holt v. State, 2010-Ohio-6529, ¶ 9 (10th Dist.). 
Summary judgment is appropriate only when the moving party demonstrates: (1) no 
genuine issue of material fact exists; (2) the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter 
of law; and (3) reasonable minds could come to but one conclusion and that conclusion is 
adverse to the party against whom the motion for summary judgment is made, that party 
being entitled to have the evidence most strongly construed in its favor. Civ.R. 56(C); State 
ex rel. Grady v. State Emp. Relations Bd., 78 Ohio St.3d 181, 183 (1997). 
No. 26AP-359 4 

{¶ 9} Pursuant to Civ.R. 56(C), the moving party bears the initial burden of 
informing the trial court of the basis for the summary judgment motion and of identifying 
those portions of the record demonstrating the absence of a genuine issue of material fact. 
Dresher v. Burt, 75 Ohio St.3d 280, 292-93 (1996). The moving party cannot discharge its 
initial burden with a conclusory assertion that the nonmoving party has no evidence to 
prove its case; the moving party must specifically point to evidence of the type listed in 
Civ.R. 56(C) affirmatively demonstrating the nonmoving party has no evidence to support 
the nonmoving party’s claims. Id. at 293; Vahila v. Hall, 77 Ohio St.3d 421, 429 (1997). If 
the moving party fails to satisfy its initial burden, the court must deny the motion for 
summary judgment. Dresher at 293. Where the moving party satisfies the initial burden, 
summary judgment is appropriate unless the nonmoving party responds, by affidavit or 
otherwise, as provided under Civ.R. 56, with specific facts demonstrating a genuine issue 
exists for trial. Id.; Hall v. Ohio State Univ. College of Humanities, 2012-Ohio-5036, ¶ 12 
(10th Dist.); Civ.R. 56(E). 
IV. Analysis 
{¶ 10} Ms. He’s three assignments of error are interrelated, and we address them 
jointly. In her first assignment of error, Ms. He a rgues the trial court erred in granting 
summary judgment in favor of U.S. Bank when genuine issues of material fact remained. 
In her second assignment of error, Ms. He argues the trial court erred in failing to consider 
evidence of the existence of a loan modification agreement. In her third assignment of 
error, Ms. He argues the trial court erred in granting summary judgment because the 
arrears calculation was inconsistent with the loan modification agreement. Taken together, 
these three assignments of error assert the trial court erred in granting summary judgment 
in favor of U .S. Bank because there remained a genuine issue of material fact as to the 
existence of a genuine loan modification agreement. 
{¶ 11} To prevail on a motion for summary judgment in a foreclosure action, a 
plaintiff must present Civ.R. 56 evidentiary materials establishing: “ ‘(1) that the plaintiff is 
the holder of the note and mortgage, or is a partly entitled to enforce the instrument; (2) if 
the plaintiff is not the original mortgagee, the chain of assignments and transfers; (3) that 
the mortgagor is in default; (4) that all conditions precedent have been met; and (5) the 
No. 26AP-359 5 

amount of principal and interest due.’ ” U.S. Bank Natl. Assn. v. Lewis, 2019-Ohio-3014, 
¶ 23 (10th Dist.), quoting Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v. Najar, 2013-Ohio-1657, ¶ 17 
(8th Dist.). 
{¶ 12} In support of its motion for summary judgment, U.S. Bank presented the note 
and mortgage documents, the assignment of the mortgage, the payment history, a default 
letter sent to Ms. He, and the affidavit of the records custodian establishing Ms. He 
defaulted under the terms of the loan and did not cure the default, the loan was accelerated, 
and the amount due on the loan. Thus, U.S. Bank submitted Civ.R. 56 evidentiary materials 
demonstrating each element of its foreclosure claim, satisfying its burden in support of its 
motion for summary judgment. See Lewis at ¶ 23 (“In a foreclosure action, presentation of 
the note and mortgage documents, along with the affidavit of a loan servicing agent or 
employee with personal knowledge of the account, may provide sufficient evidentiary 
support for a summary judgment in favor of the mortgagee.”). 
{¶ 13} Ms. He does not dispute U.S. Bank met its initial burden under Civ.R. 56. 
Instead, Ms. He asserts the trial court erred in granting summary judgment because there 
remained a genuine issue of material fact as to the existence of a loan modification 
agreement. In response to U.S. Bank’s motion for summary judgment, Ms. He filed a 
memorandum contra along with her own affidavit, a timeline of her communications with 
the loan servicers, and five pages of a document she claims are the relevant portions of the 
purported loan modification agreement. U.S. Bank asserts these materials contain 
inadmissible hearsay and are not true and accurate copies of documents because they are 
incomplete. However, even assuming the materials are admissible, Ms. He does not point 
to anything in these pages setting forth the terms of the purported loan modification that 
would alter U.S. Bank’s contractual right to enforce the note and mortgage or that Ms. He 
cured the default. 
{¶ 14} Among the materials Ms. He submitted in response to U.S. Bank’s motion for 
summary judgment is a document Ms. He describes as containing the “relevant portions” 
of the loan modification agreement. This document consists of five pages. The first page 
references an “enclosed modification agreement,” but Ms. He did not submit the remaining 
pages of the document containing the terms of the modification itself. (Memo Contra, Ex. 
A at 1.) The document expressly states Ms. He is in default under the note and mortgage 
No. 26AP-359 6 

and U.S. Bank will “complete/resume our collection action as necessary, including 
foreclosure” if Ms. He fails to properly execute or perform under the proposed modification 
agreement. (Memo Contra, Ex. A at 1.) The remaining four pages she submitted are various 
signature pages showing Ms. He’s signature, the date of August 1, 2024, and the seal of a 
notary public. 
{¶ 15} None of these pages include the terms of the proposed modification, and Ms. 
He does not point to any other Civ.R. 56 materials establishing the terms of the proposed 
modification or demonstrating Ms. He otherwise cured the default . Construing the 
evidence in a light most favorable to Ms. He, these materials, at most, create a mere 
possibility that a loan modification agreement could have existed between the parties. The 
documents do not demonstrate the terms of such loan modification agreement, whether 
and how the terms of the loan modification agreement altered the terms of the note and 
mortgage and impacted U.S. Bank’s ability to enforce the not

leads.text:
SECOND DIVISION
DOYLE, P. J.,
DAVIS and WHITAKER, JJ.
NOTICE: Motions for reconsideration must be
received no later than 4:30 pm on the 10th day after
the decision was issued to be deemed timely filed. 
https://www.gaappeals.gov/rules
October 20, 2026
In the Court of Appeals of Georgia
A26A0941. BLACKWELL et al. v. 5 AIF JUNIPER 2, LLC.
DAVIS, Judge.
Carson Blackwell seeks review following a bench trial in this ownership dispute
over a one-acre property in Gwinnett County, Georgia. On appeal, Blackwell argues
that (1) the trial court erred by denying his request for a jury trial; (2) 5 AIF Juniper
2, LLC (“5 AIF Juniper”) lacked standing to bring this lawsuit because it is not
licensed to do business in Georgia and because it had sold the disputed property by the
time of trial; and (3) the trial court erred by reforming a deed of sale and security deed
to include the one-acre parcel. For the reasons that follow, we affirm.
“On an appeal from an entry of judgment following a bench trial, we apply a de
novo standard of review to any questions of law decided by the trial court, but will
defer to any factual findings made by that court if there is any evidence to sustain
them.” Harris v. W. Cent. Ga. Bank, 335 Ga. App. 114, 114 (779 SE2d 441) (2015).
So viewed, the record shows that, in 2014, Blackwell purchased a 7.25-acre
parcel of undeveloped land in Gwinnett County for $89,000 with the intention to
build a house on the property. The parcel of land was triangular in shape and
surrounded a separate 1-acre undeveloped parcel. After Blackwell completed an
environmental and soil study, however, Blackwell learned that it would be
prohibitively expensive to build a house on the property as it then existed. As a result,
Blackwell purchased the middle 1-acre property for $13,000. 
Blackwell then prepared a site plan that showed the proposed house and septic
drain field located across both parcels. A revised site plan was prepared in June 2015
that showed both parcels in one combined lot, and Gwinnett County approved a
combination plat and assigned one tax identification number and address for the
combined lot. Blackwell recorded the combination plat and intended for the parcels
to be consolidated into one property. Blackwell proceeded to build a house that sat
primarily on the one-acre parcel but spanned across the former boundary lines of the
two parcels. Blackwell, however, did not complete the home for financial reasons, and
2
in 2018, he conveyed the 7.25 acre property to his business, The Right Touch
Painters, LLC. 
Eventually, in 2018, The Right Touch Painters entered into a purchase and sale
agreement to sell “the following house and land” for $700,000 to RW Investments,
LLC. Under the purchase agreement, Blackwell agreed to sell the property “with the
home built before closing,” “with a completed basement,” with “insulation to be
installed in the home,” with “selections of options for the home,” and with a right to
inspect the home, and he agreed to “convey good and marketable title to the Home
by limited warranty deed.” RW Investments obtained a loan from 5 Arch Funding
Corp. to finance the transaction through a security deed on the property.1 However,
the security deed and warranty deed stated that Blackwell conveyed only 7.25 acres,
not the 8.25 acres combined. Eventually, in 2021, the property was foreclosed upon,
and 5 AIF Juniper purchased the property at the foreclosure sale. 
5 AIF Juniper filed the instant lawsuit, seeking to quiet title to the property and
reform the deeds to reflect that the entire 8.25 acre combined parcel was conveyed as
part of the sale, as well as raising claims for trespass and ejectment. Following a bench
1 The security deed was eventually assigned to 5 AIF Juniper. 
3
trial, the trial court concluded that the evidence “clearly, unequivocally, and
decisively showed that a mutual mistake occurred with regard to the legal description”
of the property in the deeds. Accordingly, the trial court ordered that the deeds be
reformed to reflect that the entire 8.25-acre parcel was conveyed during the 2018 sale.2
Blackwell filed a motion for new trial, which the trial court denied, and this appeal
followed. 
1. Blackwell first argues that the trial court erred by denying his request for a
jury trial. The trial court did not err by denying the request because there is no right
to a jury trial in equity proceedings.
“The right of trial by jury as declared by the Constitution of the state or as given
by a statute of the state shall be preserved to the parties inviolate.” OCGA § 9-11-38.
“However, it is well-settled that there is no constitutional right to a jury trial in equity
cases in Georgia.” Mancuso v. Jackson, 359 Ga. App. 428, 429 (858 SE2d 244) (2021).
And “[g]enerally, there is no statutory right to trial by jury in equity cases.” Id.
(quotation marks omitted). Here, before the bench trial, the trial court stated on the
2 Although the trial court noted that other claims remained pending, it certified
its order as final under OCGA § 9-11-54(b). 
4
record that a special master resolved any quiet title issues,3 and so the sole issue to be
resolved at the bench trial was the claim to reform the deed based on a mutual mistake,
which is an equitable claim. DeGolyer v. Green Tree Servicing, LLC, 291 Ga. App. 444,
447(1) (662 SE2d 141) (2008) (“In all cases where the form of the conveyance or
instrument is, by mutual mistake, contrary to the intention of the parties in their
contract, equity will interfere to make it conform thereto.”); OCGA § 23-2-25.
Because only an equitable claim remained, Blackwell did not have a right to a jury trial,
and the trial court did not err by denying the request for one.
Rather than point to a particular constitutional provision or statute beyond the
general right to a jury trial in the Civil Practice Act to support his claim that he was
entitled to a jury trial, Blackwell instead points to two cases where jury trials were had
in equity cases - Livingston v. Barnett, 193 Ga. 640 (19 SE2d 385) (1942), and Tidwell
3 We note that no proceedings before a special master, nor any orders or
findings by the special master, are in the record on appeal. “It is well established that
the burden is on the party alleging error to show it affirmatively by the record.” Mays
v. Ed Voyles Chrysler-Plymouth, Inc., 255 Ga. App. 357, 359(2) (565 SE2d 515) (2002).
Thus, to the extent Blackwell seeks to rely on any part of the special master
proceedings to support his claims of error, we cannot consider them and must
presume that the trial court and/or the special master acted appropriately because
“[w]e will not presume error from a silent record.” State v. Cooper, 271 Ga. App. 771,
772 (611 SE2d 90) (2005).
5
v. Bassett, 271 Ga. App. 867 (611 SE2d 123) (2005). Neither case is availing. As an
initial matter, neither case specifically holds that there is a right to jury trials in equity
proceedings or proceedings to reform a deed, as each opinion instead merely describes
cases where a jury trial was held. “[Q]uestions which merely lurk in the record,
neither brought to the attention of the court nor ruled upon, are not to be considered
as having been so decided as to constitute precedents.” State v. Sanford, 312 Ga. 707,
710 (864 SE2d 448) (2021). Second, it is well-settled that, even though no right to a
jury trial exists in equity cases, “a superior court judge may choose to use a jury to
return a special verdict in an equity case with disputed issues of material fact.” Cotton
v. Vinings Estates Cmty. Ass’n, Inc., 379 Ga. App. 533, 546(5) (930 SE2d 90) (2026)
(quotation marks omitted). But “[a]lthough a trial court trying a suit [in equity] may
empanel a jury to render special verdicts, the court is not required to do so.” Turner
Advertising Co. v. Garcia, 251 Ga. 46, 48(4) (302 SE2d 547) (1983). Thus, the
existence of cases where jury trials were held in equity cases does not mean that there
is a right to a jury trial in such cases, nor does it mean that the trial court erred by
denying Blackwell’s request for a jury trial here. See Montana v. Blount, 232 Ga. App.
782, 786(1)(b) (504 SE2d 447) (1998) (“[A] jury sits in equity only in an advisory
6
capacity to the trial judge, [and] it was not error for the trial court either to determine
that there existed nothing for which the jury could render an advisory verdict, or to
decide to try the case without the jury and find that Montana was not entitled to
equitable relief.”). 
2. Blackwell also argues that 5 AIF Juniper lacked standing to bring this lawsuit
and to have judgment entered in its favor.4 He argues that 5 AIF Juniper lacks standing
because (1) it did not properly register as a company doing business in Georgia with
the Secretary of State; and (2) it sold the property before trial, thereby leaving it with
no interest in the property. We conclude that Blackwell has not shown that 5 AIF
Juniper lacked standing.
(a) By statute, a foreign corporation transacting business in this state is required
to obtain a certificate of authority from the Georgia Secretary of State, subject to
certain exceptions. OCGA § 14-2-1501(a). As relevant to this case, “[a] foreign
corporation transacting business in this state without a certificate of authority may not
maintain a proceeding in any court in this state until it obtains a certificate of
authority.” OCGA § 14-2-1502(a) (emphasis supplied). 
4 We address Blackwell’s enumerations of error in a different order than that
presented in his brief.
7
Here, it appears to be undisputed that 5 AIF Juniper is not a Georgia
corporation, nor does it have a certificate of authority. Thus, it may only maintain a
court proceeding if it is not “transacting business” in Georgia.
Whether one is transacting business for purposes of the applicable
statutes should be decided on a case-by-case basis and not by application
of a mechanical rule. Under such test it is the extent of activities by the
foreign corporation in Georgia rather than the singleness that is
considered, whether it be a construction enterprise or some other
business. Where the activities are minimal and unsubstantial in
connection with only one contract and there is displayed no intention to
continue these activities after completion of the single contract, the
foreign corporation does not have to qualify because its contracts with
Georgia relate to an isolated transaction. If such activities are extensive
in scope and involve a great deal of work over a period of time, then
qualification is required despite all such activities being related to a single
contract.
Universal Indus. Gases, Inc. v. Action Indus., Inc., 361 Ga. App. 282, 284 (864 SE2d
121) (2021) (quotation marks omitted). “[T]he defendant has the burden of proving
the facts necessary to obtain a dismissal” based on the lack of a certificate of authority.
Id. at 283 (emphasis omitted).
8
Here, the only fact to which Blackwell points on appeal that he alleges shows
that 5 AIF Juniper is transacting business in Georgia is its actions in prosecuting this
case.5 The certificate of authority statute, however, delineates certain activities that
do not constitute transacting business, which include “[m]aintaining or defending any
action[,]” “[o]wning, without more, real or personal property;” and “[c]onducting
an isolated transaction not in the course of a number of repeated transactions of a like
nature.” OCGA § 14-2-1501(a)(1), (9)-(10). Thus, we cannot say that 5 AIF Juniper
is “transacting business” in Georgia merely by obtaining the security deed, purchasing
the disputed property at a foreclosure sale, and then participating in this property
dispute. See Powder Springs Holdings, LLC v. RL BB ACQ II-GA PSH, LLC, 325 Ga.
App. 694, 696(1) (754 SE2d 655) (2014) (under materially identical statute that applies
to limited liability companies, defendant LLC was not required to obtain certificate of
authority when record evidence showed its busi

leads.caseName: Doshynko Sullivan v. FP Glenwood, LLC
leads.court: Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
leads.text:
NOT FOR PUBLICATION 

In the 
United States Court of Appeals 
For the Eleventh Circuit 
____________________ 
No. 26-11146 
Non-Argument Calendar 
____________________ 

DOSHYNKO SULLIVAN, 
Plaintiﬀ-Appellant, 
versus 

FP GLENWOOD, LLC, 
FAROS PROPERTY MANAGEMENT LLC, 
Defendants-Appellees. 
 ____________________ 
Appeal from the United States District Court 
for the Northern District of Georgia 
D.C. Docket No. 1:24-cv-01439-MHC 
____________________ 

Before NEWSOM, GRANT, and WILSON, Circuit Judges. 
PER CURIAM: 
USCA11 Case: 26-11146 Document: 28-1 Date Filed: 10/20/2026 Page: 1 of 10 
2 Opinion of the Court 26-11146 
Doshynko Sullivan sued FP Glenwood ( his landlord) and 
Faros Property Management (his property manager), alleging that 
their negligence led to a fire in his bedroom . While opposing 
summary judgment, Sullivan sought to introduce expert testimony 
about the cause of the fire. But the district court issued an order 
excluding that testimony and granting summary judgment for FP 
Glenwood and Faros. See Sullivan v. FP Glenwood, LLC , No. 1:24 -
CV-1439-MHC, 2026 WL 1105013, at *10 (N.D. Ga. Mar. 9, 2026). 
Sullivan now appeals both parts of that order . We affirm the 
district court. 
I. 
Sullivan lived in an apartment owned by FP Glenwood and 
managed by Faros. At one point, he was having issues with a light 
fixture in his bedroom , and over the course of a week submitted 
two work orders about it. He first complained that the fixture 
would trip the apartment’s electricity, and eventually that it would 
not work at all. About a month after his second complaint, the 
light fixture was replaced. Thereafter, Sullivan filed no complaints 
about the light, though it still occasionally flickered. 
A little over a month after the light was replaced , Sullivan’s 
apartment tragically caught fire. While he was not home at the 
time of the fire, he believed that improper repair of the light fixture 
was the cause. 
Battalion Chief and incident commander Winfred Smith 
responded to the scene. Based on the charring patterns, h e 
believed that the fire was an electrical one that began near the light 
USCA11 Case: 26-11146 Document: 28-1 Date Filed: 10/20/2026 Page: 2 of 10 
26-11146 Opinion of the Court 3 
fixture, and he documented that observation in an NFIRS (National 
Fire Incident Reporting System) report. But Chief Smith also 
explained that his findings were merely “preliminary”; his role was 
just to decide whether experts were needed to further investigate. 
Consistent with his preliminary role, Chief Smith’s investigation 
was limited, even though at one point he made a stray suggestion 
about having formed his opinion to a “reasonable degree of 
engineering certainty.” To name a few self-admitted limitations, 
he did not use “the scientific method,” employ National Fire 
Protection Association protocols, or “conduct any experiments” on 
fire origin. Neither did Chief Smith analyze the circuit breakers 
(despite conceding that a fire -origin investigation “probably 
needed” to do so), nor did he evaluate the electrical panel. He also 
could not exclude alternative causes of the fire, such as “electrical 
components in the unit” or a “defect in the power supply.” 
Fire investigator Corey Smith also analyzed the fire. After 
speaking with individuals on the scene, taking photos, reviewing 
burn patterns, and employing the scientific method, he could not 
determine its cause. He also could not, to a reasonable degree of 
certainty, exclude the apartment’s electrical components, a power 
surge, or a circuit-breaker issue as potential causes. 
Two years later , Sullivan sued , alleging that FP Glenwood 
and Faros caused the fire by negligently maintaining and repairing 
the light. In opposing summary judgment , Sullivan sought to 
introduce Chief Smith’s opinion. But in one order, the district 
court excluded both Chief Smith’s causation testimony and granted 
USCA11 Case: 26-11146 Document: 28-1 Date Filed: 10/20/2026 Page: 3 of 10 
4 Opinion of the Court 26-11146 
summary judgment for FP Glenwood and Faros. See Sullivan, 2026 
WL 1105013, at *10. Sullivan appeals that order. 
II. 
A district court’s decision to admit or exclude expert 
testimony is reviewed for abuse of discretion . United States v. 
Frazier, 387 F.3d 1244, 1258 (11th Cir. 2004) . Under this “very 
limited” form of review, we defer to the district court unless its 
decision was “manifestly erroneous” or used “ the wrong legal 
standard.” Id. at 1259 (quotation omitted). 
A grant of summary judgment is reviewed de novo . 
McCreight v. AuburnBank, 117 F.4th 1322, 1329 (11th Cir. 2024). 
Summary judgment requires a movant to show that there is “no 
genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled 
to judgment as a matter of law.” Id. (quoting Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(a)). 
If a reasonable jury could find for the nonmoving party, a “genuine 
issue of material fact exists.” Id. (quotation omitted). We view the 
evidence and all reasonable inferences in the light most favorable 
to the nonmoving party. Id. 
III. 
We start with the district court’s decision to exclude Chief 
Smith’s testimony and then turn to the grant of summary 
judgment for FP Glenwood and Faros. 
A. 
The admissibility of expert testimony in federal court is 
governed by Federal Rule of Evidence 702 and the Supreme 
USCA11 Case: 26-11146 Document: 28-1 Date Filed: 10/20/2026 Page: 4 of 10 
26-11146 Opinion of the Court 5 
Court’s opinion in Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals , Inc. See 
509 U.S. 579 (1993) . Our cases interpreting Rule 702 require an 
expert to be qualified to testify, use a reliable methodology, and 
offer testimony useful to the factfinder. See Frazier, 387 F.3d at 
1260. In administering these requirements, district courts perform 
a “critical gatekeeping function” and ensure that substandard 
expert testimony is excluded . I d. (quotation omitted) . Careful 
inquiry into expert testimony is needed because “of the powerful 
and potentially misleading effect of expert evidence.” Id. at 1263. 
The dispute over Chief Smith’s causation testimony 
concerns the second prong of Rule 702’s three- part test: the 
reliability of his methods . Generally speaking and “to the extent 
practicable,” reliable methodology requires theories and 
techniques that are testable, peer -reviewed, published, well-
pedigreed, and subject to measurable error rates. Id. at 1262; accord 
Daubert, 509 U.S. at 593-94. 
Given the limited nature of Chief Smith’s investigation, the 
district court did not abuse its discretion by determining tha t his 
testimony was not reliable. As conceded by Chief Smith himself , 
his opinion was based on visual observation instead of an analysis 
of electrical evidence, an exclusion of other reasonable causes, or 
the use of recognized protocols for fire investigation. Indeed, Chief 
Smith expressly disclaimed using the “scientific method ,” nor did 
he analyze the circuit breakers even though he thought any fire-
origin analysis “probably needed” to do so. Considering this, the 
USCA11 Case: 26-11146 Document: 28-1 Date Filed: 10/20/2026 Page: 5 of 10 
6 Opinion of the Court 26-11146 
district court was not “manifestly” wrong to exclude Smith’s 
testimony. Frazier, 387 F.3d at 1258 (quotation omitted). 
Sullivan’s arguments do not show otherwise. He first argues 
that courts have recognized that “the very methodology Chief 
Smith employed” can be “a valid basis for expert causation 
testimony in fire cases.” But the cited cases show the opposite. In 
United States v. Santiago, a panel held that fire causation testimony 
was admissible because the expert “systematically examined the 
scene,” “used the scientific method,” and ruled out alternative 
causes of the fire. 202 F. App ’x 399, 401 (11th Cir. 2006) 
(unpublished). And in Great Northern Insurance Co. v. Ruiz , the 
district court admitted fire causation testimony that was derived 
by—among other things— a “process of elimination.” 688 F. Supp. 
2d 1362, 1372-74 (S.D. Ga. 2010). Chief Smith, by contrast, testified 
that he did not use the scientific method or rule out alternative 
causes. 
Sullivan next relies on the fact that Chief Smith examined 
the charring on the scene, was the incident commander, completed 
an NFIRS report, and testified under oath to a “reasonable degree 
of engineering certainty” about his opinion. None of these points 
address the crux of the issue: Chief Smith did not systematically 
work through potential causes of the fire. This was not a failing on 
his part. Systematic investigation was not his role. Rather, his job 
was to make a “preliminary” determination of whether experts 
were needed for a full investigation. And despite what Sullivan 
asserts, “preliminary” is not just a semantic label; Smith himself 
USCA11 Case: 26-11146 Document: 28-1 Date Filed: 10/20/2026 Page: 6 of 10 
26-11146 Opinion of the Court 7 
stated that his investigation was limited in scope. Whatever Smith 
meant when saying he formed his opinion to a “reasonable degree 
of engineering certainty,” that phrase alone is not enough to make 
his opinion admissible. 
Sullivan’s remaining arguments also fall short. W hile 
experts may sometimes permissibly “draw a conclusion from a set 
of observations based on extensive and specialized experience,” 
Chief Smith himself conceded that his analysis had large gaps. 
Kumho Tire Co. v. Carmichael , 526 U.S. 137, 156 (1999) . And t hese 
gaps do not merely go to weight as Sullivan contends ; district 
courts must be vigilant in excluding expert testimony precisely 
“because of the difficulty in evaluating it.” Daubert, 509 U.S. at 595. 
Lastly, the supposed distinction between Chief Smith’s opinion on 
“fire origin” as opposed to “fire cause” is irrelevant because they 
are both ultimately opinions. 
In sum, both the broad leeway given to district courts to 
assess reliability and the self-described limitations of Chief Smith’s 
testimony mean we cannot say that the district court abused its 
discretion. 
 B. 
Negligence under Georgia law requires “four elements: a 
duty, a breach of that duty, causation and damages.” Johnson v. Am. 
Nat’l Red Cross, 276 Ga. 270, 272 (2003) (quotation omitted). Like 
any plaintiff, Sullivan needs to convince a jury on all elements. A 
failure to establish a dispute of fact for even one element of his 
USCA11 Case: 26-11146 Document: 28-1 Date Filed: 10/20/2026 Page: 7 of 10 
8 Opinion of the Court 26-11146 
negligence claim is thus fatal to his appeal. Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 
477 U.S. 317, 322-23 (1986). 
Sullivan cannot preclude summary judgment for FP 
Glenwood and Faros on his negligent maintenance claim because 
there is no dispute of fact about causation. Causation requires 
showing how a defendant ’s wrongdoing harmed the plaintiff . 
Redmon v. Daniel , 335 Ga. App. 159, 162- 163 (2015). But Sullivan 
has offered no specific evidence about what the wrongdoing was 
or how it caused the fire. 
On appeal, he points to the fact that (1) he reported electrical 
problems with the light fixture; (2) the fixture was replaced; (3) the 
light fixture occasionally flickered thereafter ; and (4) Chief Smith 
observed charring near the light fixture and put “Failure of 
Equipment or Heat Source” in his NFIRS report. But as the district 
court explained, these facts amount to showing that “ Plaintiff had 
issues with a light fixture in his bedroom along with many other 
issues in the Apartment, Defendants replaced the problematic light 
fixture, a fire occurred in the Apartment, and there was some 
charring near the replaced light in the ruins. ” Sullivan, 2026 WL 
1105013, at *9. Because none of these facts show what the negligent 
maintenance was or how such maintenance caused the fire, Sullivan 
cannot establish a material dispute of fact about causation. 
Contrary to what Sullivan contends, the district court did 
not apply an improperly high causation sta

 NOTICE
 This slip opinion is subject to formal revision before it is published in an
 advance sheet of the Ohio Official Reports. Readers are requested to
 promptly notify the Reporter of Decisions, Supreme Court of Ohio, 65
 South Front Street, Columbus, Ohio 43215, of any typographical or other
 formal errors in the opinion, in order that corrections may be made before
 the opinion is published.

 SLIP OPINION NO. 2026-OHIO-4073
 THE STATE EX REL . BRISTOLVILLE 25 DEVELOPER, L.L.C., ET AL. v. T HE
 VILLAGE OF LORDSTOWN ET AL .
 [Until this opinion appears in the Ohio Official Reports advance sheets, it
 may be cited as State ex rel. Bristolville 25 Developer, L.L.C. v. Lordstown,
 Slip Opinion No. 2026-Ohio-4073.]
Mandamus—Village lacks clear legal duty to proceed with review of data-center
 developer’s site plan because it is subject to ordinance placing a temporary
 moratorium on issuing of any new permits, as well as receipt and processing
 of permit applications, for proposed data centers—Relators have not shown
 a clear legal right to have developer’s site plan reviewed under
 premoratorium zoning ordinance—Gibson v. Oberlin and Fairmount Ctr.
 Co. v. Arnold distinguished—Writ denied.
 (No. 2025-1497—Submitted August 4, 2026—Decided October 20, 2026.)
 IN MANDAMUS.
 __________________
  SUPREME COURT OF OHIO

 The per curiam opinion below was joined by KENNEDY, C.J., and FISCHER,
DEWINE, BRUNNER, DETERS, HAWKINS, and SHANAHAN, JJ.

 Per Curiam.
 {¶ 1} Relators, Bristolville 25 Developer, L.L.C. (“Bristolville”) and
BHGH Properties, L.L.C., seek a writ of mandamus to compel respondents, the
Village of Lordstown and its planning-and-zoning administrator, Kellie D. Bordner
(collectively, “the village”), to perform duties under the Lordstown Codified
Ordinances in effect on October 20, 2025. We previously granted an alternative
writ. 2025-Ohio-5682. In addition to their evidence and merit briefing, relators
have filed a motion for leave to file rebuttal evidence and a motion asking us to take
judicial notice of actions taken by the Lordstown Village Council since the merit
briefing concluded in this case.
 {¶ 2} We deny relators’ motion for leave to file rebuttal evidence and grant
their motion for judicial notice. And because relators have not shown a clear legal
right to the relief they seek in this case, we deny the writ.
 I. FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND
 {¶ 3} Bristolville acquires and develops real property for construction of
large-scale data centers throughout the United States. In February 2025,
Bristolville agreed to purchase from BHGH Properties a parcel of real property
located in Lordstown on which Bristolville seeks to construct a data center. The
property is zoned for industrial use.
A. Site-Plan Review under the Lordstown Ordinance and Overview Process
 {¶ 4} Before an applicant may request a zoning permit for new construction
in Lordstown, local law requires projects to undergo a “Site Plan Review” overseen
by Lordstown’s Planning and Zoning Office. Chapter 1115 of the Lordstown
Codified Ordinances sets forth the site-plan-review process. Subject to exceptions

 2
  January Term, 2026

not applicable here, “[n]o permit for the construction . . . of any building shall be
given . . . except in conformity with a site plan approved by the Planning
Commission.” Lordstown Cod.Ord. 1115.02, available at Village of Lordstown,
Codified Ordinances of Lordstown, OH,
https://codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/lordstown/latest/lordstown_oh/0-0-0-15997
(accessed Sept. 17, 2026) [https://perma.cc/2SVE-YFYX].
 {¶ 5} To explain the preliminary steps to submitting a site plan for approval
by the Planning Commission, the Lordstown Planning and Zoning Office provides
to prospective zoning-permit applicants a two-page document titled “Overview of
Lordstown Village Site Plan Review Process” (“the Overview”). The Overview
details four steps in the process.
 {¶ 6} Under “step one,” a zoning-permit applicant must submit to the
Planning and Zoning Office drafts of a narrative outline of the project and a
“site/plot plan identifying property size, setbacks from all property lines to the
proposed facility . . . , and other project details.” Once the applicant submits these
draft materials, “the Village of Lordstown will begin the process of engaging the
Village Engineer(s) on the project.” The village engineer will then prepare and
provide to the developer a “work authorization,” which the developer must sign and
return to Lordstown as an acknowledgment of the developer’s responsibility to
reimburse Lordstown for the village engineer’s fees related to the project. When
the signed work acknowledgment is received, the village council will approve the
village engineer’s engagement on the project.
 {¶ 7} Once the village council approves the village engineer’s engagement
on the project, the Overview process moves on to “step two,” the “pre-application
meeting” required by Lordstown Cod.Ord. 1115.04(a). Under step two, before the
pre-application meeting, the developer must submit detailed project information,
including a preliminary-planning-evaluation form, a site-plan-review form, utility
plans, a storm-water-management plan, hazard/safety plans, and approvals from

 3
  SUPREME COURT OF OHIO

other regulatory entities. The Overview contemplates that after submission of these
draft materials, a pre-application meeting will occur and should include “everyone
from the Village team & everyone from the Developer’s team.”
 {¶ 8} Following the pre-application meeting, “step three” of the Overview
contemplates that the village engineer and planning-and-zoning administrator will
each provide written comments on the proposed site plan, identifying deficiencies
or additional information that is needed. Other Lordstown department heads may
also provide feedback for the developer to address. The developer is required in
step three to address all comments, questions, and concerns “by providing revised
drafts, responses, & updates.”
 {¶ 9} Once the site-plan details have been fully addressed and the draft site-
plan documents updated, the Overview process proceeds to final submission of the
site plan under “step four.” Final site-plan documents are submitted to Lordstown’s
planning-and-zoning administrator and must “address all revisions, questions,
concerns or comments from the pre-application meetings & any individual
department discussions/meetings.” The applicant must file a copy of the final site
plan with the planning-and-zoning administrator for approval by the Planning
Commission. Lordstown Cod.Ord. 1115.04(a).
 {¶ 10} Upon the developer’s filing of the final site plan, the Planning
Commission “shall review the site plan pursuant to the site plan review guidelines
set forth in [Lordstown Cod.Ord.] 1115.05.” Lordstown Cod.Ord. 1115.04(c). If
the Planning Commission approves the final submission, the applicant may file an
application for a zoning permit for the Planning and Zoning Office’s approval. Id.
No construction may begin until the zoning permit has been issued. Lordstown
Cod.Ord. 1115.02.
 B. Bristolville Initiates the Site-Plan-Review Process
 {¶ 11} On October 20, 2025, Bristolville initiated the site-plan-review
process set forth in the Lordstown Codified Ordinances. On that date, in

 4
  January Term, 2026

accordance with step one of the Overview, Bristolville hand-delivered to the
Planning and Zoning Office “the required narrative outline of the project and a
site/plot plan, among other things.” Bristolville also emailed a copy of these draft
materials to Bordner and Village Solicitor Matthew Ries the same day. The next
day, Bordner sent an email to Bristolville, informing them that

 since the Planning & Zoning Committee previously recommended
 a ban on data centers within the Village of Lordstown, which is now
 before Village Council, having just gone through second reading,
 the Planning & Zoning Office would not be able to proceed until
 Council makes a decision on the ban at the next Council meeting.

 {¶ 12} Bristolville responded to Bordner a week later, asking her to proceed
with the site-plan-review process in accordance with the Lordstown Codified
Ordinances because data centers were still permitted under Lordstown’s zoning
ordinances.
 C. Lordstown Passes Ordinance Prohibiting Data Centers
 {¶ 13} Six days later, on November 3, the Lordstown Village Council
passed Ordinance No. 57-2025, which would prohibit any data center within the
corporate boundaries of Lordstown.1 Village of Lordstown,
https://www.lordstown.com/wp-content/uploads/57-2025.pdf (accessed Sept. 17,
2026) [https://perma.cc/NU3M-YY2U]. The ordinance further provided that “[n]o

1. The ordinance defined “data center” as “a facility, used for the storage, management, and
dissemination of digital data, which houses computer, telecommunication, and/or network
equipment, systems, servers, appliances, and other associated components related to digital data
operations, and/or facility designed or modified to house networked computers and data and
transaction processing equipment and related infrastructure support equipment, including but not
limited to server farms, cloud computing hubs, and colocation centers.” Id. at § 1, Village of
Lordstown, https://www.lordstown.com/wp-content/uploads/57-2025.pdf (accessed Sept. 17, 2026)
[https://perma.cc/NU3M-YY2U].

 5
  SUPREME COURT OF OHIO

zoning permit, building permit, or certificate of occupancy shall be issued for any
use that meets the [ordinance’s] definition of a data center.” Id. at § 2b. The
ordinance was explicitly inapplicable to any data-center facility already existing or
under construction as of the ordinance’s effective date. Id. at § 8. The village
council passed the ordinance as an emergency measure, id. at § 9, and the ordinance
was to take effect on December 3, 2025, see R.C. 731.29.
 {¶ 14} Two days later, notwithstanding the village council’s passage of
Ordinance No. 57-2025, Bordner forwarded Bristolville’s October 20 draft site-
plan materials to Christopher Kogelnik, the village engineer, for his review. On
November 12, Ries emailed Bristolville’s counsel a letter responding to
Bristolville’s October 28 letter to Bordner. Ries denied that the village was refusing
to proceed with a site-plan review and stated that Bordner had been working with
Kogelnik to review Bristolville’s draft submission. Ries offered to schedule a
meeting with Bristolville to discuss issues that Kogelnik had identified in his initial
review, but Ries indicated that “the proposed project w[ould] likely be prohibited
by Village of Lordstown’s Ordinance No. 57-2025, which prohibits the
establishment and operation of data centers” in Lordstown.
 D. Relators File this Action; Lordstown Repeals the Ban
 {¶ 15} After receiving Ries’s letter, relators commenced this action. In their
complaint, relators ask for a writ of mandamus “directing Respondents . . . to follow
Lordstown Codified Ordinance 1115 by accepting, reviewing, and acting upon
Bristolville’s Submission and to do so throughout the Site Plan Review Process
under the Village’s applicable laws in effect as of October 20, 2025, when no data
center ban was in effect in the Village.” The complaint named Ries, Bordner, and
Lordstown as respondents. The village filed a motion to dismiss relators’ petition
under Civ.R. 12(B)(6) for failure to state a valid claim for relief in mandamus. We
granted the motion as to Ries; as to Border and Lordstown, we denied the motion,

 6
  January Term, 2026

ordered them to file an answer, and granted an alternative writ, setting a schedule
for the parties to submit evidence and merit briefs. 2025-Ohio-5682.
 {¶ 16} Before we issued our order granting an alternative writ, the village
council repe

Bank of New York Mellon v. Tope
THE BANK OF NEW YORK MELLON v. 
ACHYUT M. TOPE ET AL.
(AC 48862)
Moll, Westbrook and Harper, Js.
Syllabus
The named defendant, T, appealed from the trial court’s judgment of fore-
closure by sale rendered in favor of the plaintiff bank. T claimed, inter alia, 
that the court had improperly failed to impose sanctions on the plaintiff for 
its alleged noncompliance with his discovery requests. Held:
T could not prevail on his claim that the trial court erred in failing to rule 
on his motion for discovery sanctions, as the court implicitly ruled on that 
motion by granting certain relief at an evidentiary hearing, namely, allow-
ing posthearing depositions of witnesses and for the parties to address the 
discovery dispute in their posthearing briefs, and by rejecting T’s remain-
ing discovery related arguments and denying any additional relief in its 
memorandum of decision on T’s motion to open and vacate the judgment 
of foreclosure by sale.
The trial court did not abuse its discretion by declining to impose discovery 
sanctions on the plaintiff, as, although the plaintiff did not fully comply 
with T’s discovery requests, the plaintiff’s noncompliance did not violate 
any court order, T failed to demonstrate that such noncompliance was of 
the sort that would merit the severe sanction of dismissal, T did not file 
a motion to compel or otherwise request the court’s intervention prior to 
filing his motion for sanctions, and T was not prejudiced by the plaintiff’s 
noncompliance under the circumstances.
Argued September 3—officially released October 20, 2026
Procedural History
Action to foreclose a mortgage on certain of the defen-
dants’ real property, and for other relief, brought to the 
Superior Court in the judicial district of New Haven, 
where the defendants were defaulted for failure to 
appear; thereafter, the named defendant was defaulted 
for failure to plead; subsequently, the case was tried to 
the court, Hon. Thomas J. Corradino, judge trial ref-
eree, who, exercising the powers of the Superior Court, 
rendered judgment of foreclosure by sale; thereafter, the 
court, Hon. Thomas J. Corradino, judge trial referee, 
denied the named defendant’s motion to open and vacate 
the judgment, and the named defendant appealed to this 
court, Elgo and Cradle, Js., with Devlin, J., dissenting, 
Bank of New York Mellon v. Tope
which affirmed the trial court’s judgment; subsequently, 
on the granting of certification, the named defendant 
appealed to the Supreme Court, which reversed and 
remanded the case to this court with instructions to 
remand to the trial court for further proceedings con-
sistent with its opinion; on remand, the court, Abrams, 
J., denied the named defendant’s motion to open and 
vacate the judgment; thereafter, the court, Stone, J., 
rendered judgment of foreclosure by sale, and the named 
defendant appealed to this court. Affirmed.
Michael J. Habib, for the appellant (named defendant).
Jeffrey M. Knickerbocker, for the appellee (plaintiff).
Opinion
MOLL, J. This foreclosure matter returns to us on 
appeal from the Superior Court following remand from 
our Supreme Court. See Bank of New York Mellon v. 
Tope, 345 Conn. 662, 665, 286 A.3d 891 (2022). The 
defendant Achyut M. Tope1 now appeals from the trial 
court’s judgment of foreclosure by sale rendered in favor 
of the plaintiff, The Bank of New York Mellon, formerly 
known as The Bank of New York, as Successor to JPMor-
gan Chase Bank, N.A., as Trustee for Structured Asset 
Mortgage Investments II, Inc., Bear Stearns Alt-A Trust, 
Mortgage Pass-Through Certificates, Series 2004-3. The 
defendant claims that the trial court erred in not impos-
ing sanctions for the plaintiff’s alleged noncompliance 
with the defendant’s discovery requests before and after 
the evidentiary hearing ordered by our Supreme Court 
in Bank of New York Mellon v. Tope, supra, 683. We 
disagree and affirm the judgment of the trial court.
This case has an extensive, twelve year procedural his-
tory. In Bank of New York Mellon v. Tope, supra, 345 
Conn. 662, the defendant’s prior appeal from this court’s 
decision in Bank of New York Mellon v. Tope, 202 Conn.

M. Tope as the defendant.

the following facts and procedural history relevant to 
the present appeal: “On October 31, 2003, the defendant 
executed a promissory note in the amount of $134,000, 
payable to HSBC Mortgage Corporation (USA) (HSBC). 
To secure that note, the defendant mortgaged property 
located at 387 Sherman Avenue in New Haven (property) 
to HSBC. The note was later endorsed to JPMorgan Chase

“On July 17, 2014, the plaintiff filed the present action

his appearance [as a self-represented party] on October 
9, 2014, and, on October 28, 2014, he was defaulted for 
failing to plead. On November 10, 2014, the court, Hon. 
Thomas J. Corradino, judge trial referee, [rendered] a 
judgment of foreclosure by sale, with a sale date set for 
February 7, 2015.” (Internal quotation marks omitted.) 
Bank of New York Mellon v. Tope, supra, 345 Conn. 
665–66.
In 2015 and 2016, the defendant filed a series of motions 
to open the foreclosure judgment, which caused the sale 
date to be extended into 2017. Id., 666. “On January 3, 
2017, the defendant filed a motion to open and stay the 
judgment on the ground that he had obtained a financial 
audit that provides strong supporting documentation that 
the plaintiff does not have standing to pursue a foreclo-
sure action with respect to the property in this action. . . . 
On January 4, 2017, the defendant filed a motion for 
summary judgment alleging, inter alia, that the plaintiff 
lacked standing to bring this action because the plaintiff 
failed to show the proper chain of ownership, assign-
ment and control of the note and mortgage and prop-
erty with affidavits from persons with knowledge . . . . 
At the February 6, 2017 hearing on the defendant’s 
motion to open, the defendant represented to [the court, 
Avallone, J.] that the arguments in his motion to open 
and motion for summary judgment were generally the 
same. Accordingly, the court allowed the defendant, at

his request, to argue his motion for summary judgment 
at that hearing. Following extensive argument by the 
defendant, the court denied both of his motions. The 
court expressly rejected the defendant’s challenge to the 
plaintiff’s standing, stating: I’ve given you sufficient 
opportunity to make your arguments. I don’t believe that 
they hold water.” (Internal quotation marks omitted.) 
Id., 666–67. The defendant then filed several additional 
motions to dismiss that substantially relied on the same 
grounds as the January 3 and 4, 2017 motions; two were 
denied, and two were never adjudicated. Id., 667–70.
“On September 28, 2017, the defendant filed a motion 
to open and to vacate the judgment of foreclosure by sale,2 
[in which] he again argued that the plaintiff lacked stand-
ing to commence this action and [that], consequently, 
the court lacked subject matter jurisdiction over it, 
and asked that the action be dismissed in its entirety 
with prejudice. On October 16, 2017, [Judge Corradino] 
held a hearing on the defendant’s motion, at which the 
defendant again presented his argument to the court. 
On October 17, 2017, [Judge Corradino] issued an order 
denying the defendant’s motion to open and vacate the 
foreclosure judgment. . . .
“The defendant appealed to the Appellate Court3 from 
the trial court’s October 17, 2017 denial of his motion to 
open and vacate the foreclosure judgment. . . . On appeal 
to that court, the defendant claimed that the trial court

lacked standing to pursue foreclosure on the note, and,

over this action. . . .

Therefore, the Appellate Court affirmed the judgment

  Frog Bridge Development Co., LLC v. Osborne

FROG BRIDGE DEVELOPMENT COMPANY, LLC
 v. JOSEPH OSBORNE ET AL.
 (AC 48294)
 Alvord, Moll and Clark, Js.*

 Syllabus

The named defendant, O, appealed from the trial court’s judgment of pos-
session for the plaintiff in this summary process action, which was based on
O’s alleged refusal to accept the rent increase proposed by the plaintiff and
his alleged nonpayment of rent. O raised various special defenses, including
that he was protected under the statute (§ 47a-23c) that prohibits the evic-
tion of certain tenants, including those with physical or mental disabilities,
except for specified good cause, and that requires rent increases for such
tenants to be “fair and equitable.” On appeal, O claimed, inter alia, that the
trial court improperly found that the plaintiff’s proposed rent increase was
fair and equitable. Held:

The trial court did not err, as a matter of law, in determining that the
plaintiff’s proposed rent increase was “fair and equitable” under § 47a-23c
(c) (1); although those terms were not defined in § 47a-23c, they were plain
and unambiguous insofar as § 47a-23c (c) (1) expressly requires that the trial
court base its determination of whether a rent increase is “fair and equitable”
on certain statutory (§ 7-148c) criteria.

The trial court did not abuse its discretion in determining that the plaintiff’s
proposed rent increase was “fair and equitable” under § 47a-23c (c) (1), as the
court’s factual findings with respect to the criteria enumerated in § 7-148c
were not clearly erroneous; moreover, this court rejected O’s argument
that certain of the trial court’s remarks at trial were based on the court’s
own personal experiences and attitudes rather than the evidence presented.

The parties conceded, and this court agreed, that the trial court’s factual
finding that the defendant had failed to pay rent for a certain month was
clearly erroneous, and, accordingly, this court reversed in part the trial
court’s judgment and directed that court to render judgment for O on the
count of the complaint that alleged nonpayment of rent.

 Argued June 3—officially released October 20, 2026

 Procedural History

 Summary process action, brought to the Superior
Court in the judicial district of Windham, Housing Ses-
sion at Putnam, where the complaint was withdrawn
in part; thereafter, the case was tried to the court,

of the date of oral argument.

Altermatt, J.; judgment for the plaintiff, from which the
named defendant appealed to this court; subsequently,
the court, Altermatt, J., issued an articulation of its
decision. Reversed in part; judgment directed.
 Sean Patrick Eaton-Robb, with whom were Jane Kelle-

 Kenneth R. Slater, Jr., with whom was Thomas A.

 Opinion

 ALVORD, J. The defendant in this summary process
action, Joseph Osborne,1 appeals from the judgment
rendered, following a trial to the court, in favor of the
plaintiff, Frog Bridge Development Company, LLC. On
appeal, the defendant claims that the court erred (1) as a

rent increase was fair and equitable pursuant to General
Statutes § 47a-23c, (2) by making clearly erroneous fac-
tual findings, and (3) in rendering judgment on count
two of the plaintiff’s complaint.2 We agree with the
defendant’s third claim and, accordingly, reverse the
judgment in part.
 The following facts, as found by the trial court or as
undisputed in the record, and procedural history are
relevant to our resolution of this appeal. The plaintiff
and the defendant entered into a written lease for the

in Willimantic (premises) with a term of July 1, 2020,
through June 30, 2021, at a monthly rent of $900. After
the initial lease term expired, the defendant continued
residing at the premises. On or about December 27, 2023,

the premises from $900 per month to $1400 per month,
effective February 1, 2024. The notice provided that, if
the defendant did not either affirmatively renew the lease
or vacate the premises, a new month-to-month tenancy
would automatically be created, with a monthly rent of
$1550.3 The defendant did not respond to the proposal,
nor did he pay the increased monthly rent. He continued

 On March 19, 2024, the plaintiff served the defendant
with a notice to quit possession of the premises, listing

 In May 2024, the defendant filed an answer and special
defenses. Specifically, the defendant alleged, inter alia,

in a building with five or more units and that he had a

Nonpayment of rent; [or] (B) refusal to agree to a fair and equitable

sented the testimony of its property manager, Barbara

The defendant testified but did not offer any exhibits
into evidence.
 On November 26, 2024, the court rendered judgment
of possession in favor of the plaintiff, concluding in its

with respect to both counts of its complaint, namely,
the defendant’s refusal to accept a rent increase and his

claim that he was entitled to protection under § 47a-23c

Filed 10/19/26 The Waffle v. Tucker Investment Group CA2/7 
NOT TO BE PUBLISHED IN THE OFFICIAL REPORTS 

California Rules of Court, rule 8.1115(a), prohibits courts and parties from citing or relying on opinions 
not certified for publication or ordered published, except as specified by rule 8.1115(b). This opinion has 
not been certified for publication or ordered published for purposes of rule 8.1115. 

IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA 

SECOND APPELLATE DISTRICT 

DIVISION SEVEN 

THE WAFFLE, LLC, 

 Plaintiff and Appellant, 

 v. 

TUCKER INVESTMENT 
GROUP, LLC et al. 

 Defendants and 
Respondents. 

 B341347 

(Los Angeles County 
Super. Ct. No. SC129215) 

 APPEAL from a judgment of the Superior Court of 
Los Angeles County, Mark H. Epstein, Judge. Affirmed. 
 Ellis George, Eric M. George and Serli Polatoglu for 
Plaintiff and Appellant. 
 Saul Ewing, William E. Adams and Matthew A. Young for 
Defendants and Respondents. 
__________________________ 

2 
The Waffle, LLC appeals from a judgment in favor of 
William Tucker and Tucker Investment Group, LLC (TIG; 
collectively, the Tucker defendants) after the trial court granted 
the Tucker defendants’ motion to confirm an arbitration award in 
their favor and denied The Waffle’s motion to vacate the award. 
The Waffle contends the trial court erred because the arbitrator 
exceeded the scope of his authority by relying on findings made 
by the court in phase I of a trial on related issues; failed to issue 
a “reasoned award” that addressed the principal argument raised 
by The Waffle; and erred in awarding attorneys’ fees for work 
performed on behalf of defendants who had settled. We affirm. 

FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND 

A. The Restaurant Lease and Notice of Breach 
Tucker is the managing member of TIG. In 2014 TIG 
signed a 10-year master lease under which it leased a commercial 
property in Westwood, Los Angeles (the premises). In 2016 or 
2017 Tucker and The Waffle began negotiating a potential 
sublease of the premises with The Waffle’s principal, Gavin 
Polone. The Waffle had an existing restaurant in Hollywood and 
sought to open a second location in Westwood. On March 30, 
2017 TIG and The Waffle entered a 10-year lease for a restaurant 
space on the premises (the lease). Under an addendum to the 
lease and an attached construction work letter, TIG agreed to 
provide a “4-inch grease waste line connected to a 3000 gallon 
grease interceptor in compliance with code” (the interceptor). 
The lease did not contain a deadline to install the interceptor or 
require installation before TIG delivered possession of the 
premises to The Waffle. 

3 
Instead, the lease contained a cure provision that provided 
time limits for performance of TIG’s obligations under the lease 
upon a claimed breach by The Waffle. Section 13.6, 
subsection (a), provided: “Lessor shall not be deemed in breach of 
this Lease unless Lessor fails within a reasonable time to 
perform an obligation required to be performed by 
Lessor. . . . [A] reasonable time shall in no event be less than 
30 days after receipt by Lessor . . . of written notice specifying 
wherein such obligation of Lessor has not been performed; 
provided, however, that if the nature of Lessor’s obligation is 
such that more than 30 days are reasonably required for its 
performance, then Lessor shall not be in breach if performance is 
commenced within such 30 day period and thereafter diligently 
pursued to completion.” Section 31 of the lease provided 
attorneys’ fees to the prevailing party in any action or proceeding 
involving the premises. 
After the parties signed the lease, TIG’s project manager, 
Johnnie Morgan of Coastline Construction Management, Inc. 
(collectively, the Coastline defendants), started to analyze the 
feasibility of installing the interceptor in an elevated area behind 
the premises. From late 2017 to early 2018, TIG, Tucker, 
Morgan, Polone, The Waffle’s architect, and The Waffle’s 
mechanical and plumbing engineer discussed the feasibility of 
installing the interceptor at the premises. The viability of the 
installation was impacted by the interceptor’s large size, location 
(which required excavation of the slope behind the premises), and 
installation costs. Morgan also reached out to the City of Los 
Angeles Sanitation and Environment Department to discuss the 
interceptor, and he arranged a site visit by the City. Given the 
challenges to install the interceptor, the parties discussed as an 

4 
alternative a Schier grease trap (the Schier). The Waffle 
remained skeptical that the Schier was an acceptable alternative. 
On December 11, 2017 Morgan emailed The Waffle’s 
architect with plumbing plans that included the Schier instead of 
the interceptor. Tucker and Polone continued to discuss the 
Schier as an alternative to the interceptor. Polone expressed 
skepticism that the Schier would work given the amount of 
grease the restaurant would produce, and Tucker explained that 
the Schier was feasible and would not pose the same challenges 
as the interceptor. On February 15, 2018 Polone emailed Tucker 
that he had “‘no reason to think your proposal for substituting 
the [interceptor] called for in our agreement for the Schier unit 
will be acceptable.’” Tucker responded on February 17, “‘I don’t 
understand why you are not open to being cooperative and 
reasonable . . . . [Y]ou seem to say that you now won’t work with 
us even if [the Schier] is shown to be a great option.’” On 
March 9 Polone emailed Tucker, “‘[W]e must resolve the issues 
with the . . . grease interceptor.’” 
On March 19, 2018 The Waffle sent Tucker a letter (the 
notice) providing “notice of your breach of our March 30, 2017 
Lease.” The notice cited the requirement in the lease to provide 
the interceptor and explained The Waffle refused to sign off on 
the plans for the premises because the Tucker defendants did 
“not provide for the required 3,000 gallon grease [interceptor].” 
The notice concluded, “We ask that you instead provide plans 
consistent with the [construction] [w]ork [l]etter and the Lease, 
and because to date you have failed to do so, we are providing 
this notice per Section 13.6(a) of our Lease.” The next day Tucker 
sent Polone a letter to confirm receipt of the notice, in which he 
explained that TIG had not inserted the Schier into the plans. 

5 
Tucker added, “‘[W]e understood you had reserved your rights 
with respect to the grease interceptor to be installed. We were 
simply request[ing] [the plans] be initialed’” per the terms of the 
lease. 
After further discussions, on April 6, 2018 Polone emailed 
Tucker to decline the Schier as an alternative, stating, “As I have 
said many times, I did not think this substitution would be 
acceptable and this decision is now final.” Tucker responded, 
“FYI, I’m now going back to engineers about installing the 3,000-
gallon [interceptor].” Tucker then spoke with both a plumbing 
engineer and a civil engineer about the interceptor. On April 16 
Tucker emailed Polone to state he was “‘interviewing shoring 
engineers for the design work of both the [interceptor] and the 
structural impact on the building. Will keep you posted when we 
know more about the timeline.’” 

B. The Lawsuit and Stipulation To Bifurcate Trial 
On May 2, 2018 The Waffle filed a lawsuit against the 
Tucker and Coastline defendants. The operative third amended 
complaint alleged causes of action against the Tucker and 
Coastline defendants for fraud and negligent misrepresentation 
and against TIG for rescission, breach of written contract, and 
declaratory relief. The Waffle alleged with respect to the fraud 
and negligent misrepresentation causes of action that the 
defendants acted fraudulently before and after executing the 
lease, made false promises, and concealed and misrepresented 
key issues relating to the grease interceptor.1 On 

1 TIG subsequently filed a cross-complaint against The 
Waffle for breach of the lease and related causes of action, which 
it later voluntarily dismissed. 

6 
November 16, 2021 the parties stipulated to bifurcate the trial, 
with a bench trial on the breach of contract cause of action 
against TIG (phase I) and a subsequent jury trial on the 
remaining causes of action against the Tucker and Coastline 
defendants (phase II). 

C. Phase I: The Bench Trial on the Breach of Contract Cause of 
Action 
In November 2021 the trial court held a six-day bench trial 
on The Waffle’s breach of contract cause of action against TIG. 
On December 6, 2021 the court orally announced its ruling. The 
court explained that under the “odd” language in section 13.6, 
subsection (a), of the lease, “even if there is a clear failure by the 
landlord to perform an unambiguous requirement in the contract 
that the landlord is required to do, it is still not a breach . . . until 
the tenant gives the landlord notice, specifies the duty that the 
landlord has not yet performed, and 30 days has expired subject 
to the [condition allowing for additional time if the duty cannot 
be cured in 30 days].” Under the lease, therefore, the landlord is 
not in breach unless “it is not finished within 30 days,” or, if the 
duty cannot be reasonably completed in 30 days, “it is not 
commenced within 30 days and thereafter diligently pursued.” 
Because installation of the interceptor “was not a 30-day cure,” 
TIG “need[ed] to commence [installation] within 30 days and 
diligently proceed thereafter to completion.” The court explained 
Tucker “did do something. He did start. He did say, ‘I will talk 
to the engineers,’ and he did talk to his team. He did talk to 
Mr. Morgan. And he did say, ‘Okay. We are going to have to go 
with the 3,000-gallon grease interceptor.’” Tucker “had given up 
on the Schier grease [interceptor] . . . and had instructed 

7 
Mr. Morgan to move forward with putting in the 3,000-gallon 
grease interceptor.” The court found TIG did not breach the lease 
and ruled in favor of TIG on the breach of contract cause of 
action. 

D. Phase II: The Jury Trial on the Remaining Causes of 
Action 
In March and April 2022, the trial court held a jury trial on 
The Waffle’s fraud and negligent misrepresentation causes of 
action against the Tucker and Coastline defendants. During the 
trial the parties presented their arguments; called witnesses, 
including experts; and presented documentary evidence of the 
parties’ communications. The court excluded any mention of the 
disposition of phase I of the trial. On April 4, 2022 the jury 
returned a verdict for the Coastline defendants on The Waffle’s 
negligent misrepresentation claim but was deadlocked on the 
remaining causes of action against the Tucker defendants (for 
fraudulent and negligent misrepresentation) and the Coastline 
defendants (for fraudulent misrepresentation), resulting in a 
mistrial. Instead of retrying the remaining causes of action 
against the Tucker and Coastline defendants, the parties agreed 
to arbitrate the claims. 

E. The Stipulation To Arbitrate 
On June 28, 2022 the parties signed a stipulation agreeing 
to “submit all remaining claims and issues (including any 
motions for attorney fees) in the above-captioned litigation to 
private binding arbitration.” The stipulation directed the 
arbitrator to apply the substantive law of California on the 
merits and “follow the procedural rules of ADR Services, Inc.” 

8 
The parties agreed to “waive any right to appeal the decisions 
made during the action, and further agree[d] to be bound by the 
determination of the arbitrator absent evidence of any activities 
described in California Code of Civil Procedure Section 1286.2.”2 
The stipulation “permitted” and “encouraged” the “use as 
evidence during arbitration the written discovery, documents, 
deposition transcripts and trial transcripts exchanged and 
prepared during the action” and “deemed admitted for purposes 
of arbitration

IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF OHIO 
ELEVENTH APPELLATE DISTRICT 
GEAUGA COUNTY 

U.S. BANK NATIONAL

MEMORANDUM OPINION AND JUDGMENT ENTRY 

Decided: October 19, 2026 
Judgment: Appeal dismissed 

Suzanne M. Godenswager , and David T. Brady , Sandhu Law Group, L.L.C., 1213

Andrew M. Engel , Whitney E. Kaster , and Marc E. Dann , Dann Law, 15000 Madison

ROBERT J. PATTON, J. 
{¶1} Defendant-appellant, Theresa A. Shaffer (“Shaffer”), appeals from the trial 
court’s decision granting plaintiff -appellee, U.S. Bank National Association ’s, as trustee 
of NRZ Pass-Through Trust XI (“U.S. Bank National”), motion for summary judgment on 
its complaint for foreclosure. 

PAGE 2 OF 9 

Case No. 2025-G-0031 
{¶2} Upon review, we conclude that the trial court’s judgment and decree of 
foreclosure is not a final appealable order. The appeal is dismissed. 
Substantive and Procedural Facts 
{¶3} On June 12, 2024, U.S. Bank National filed a Complaint for money, 
foreclosure, and other equitable relief against Shaffer, Brian Shaffer (“Brian”), and their 
unknown spouses .1 The complaint also named Capital One National Association, The 
Huntington National Bank, LCE Federal Credit Union, John Carro ll University, and the 
Geauga County Treasurer. According to the complaint, Shaffer owed U.S. Bank National 
$142,118.85 on the note and mortgage with interest at the annual rate of 6.65% from 
March 1, 2018. 
{¶4} John Carroll University filed its answer on July 8, 2024. LCE Federal Credit 
Union filed its answer on August 2, 2024. Shaffer and Brian jointly filed their answer on 
September 8, 2024. 
{¶5} On December 12, 2024, U.S. Bank National filed a motion for default 
judgment against Ca pital One National Association, The Huntington National Bank, 
successor by merger to Sky Bank, and John Doe, Name Unknown, Unknown Spouse, if 
any of Theresa A. Shaffer. The same day, U.S. Bank National filed a motion for summary 
judgment on the claims against Shaffer and Brian. Shaffer and Brian jointly filed a 
response in opposition to U.S. Bank National’s motion for summary judgment on February 
13, 2025. 

1. The Unknown Spouse of Brian Shaffer, as designated in the complaint, was dismissed from the action 
on December 3, 2024. 

PAGE 3 OF 9 

Case No. 2025-G-0031 
{¶6} On March 18, 2025, Shaffer and Brian also filed a joint motion for summary 
judgment wherein they argued that the complaint was barred by the statute of limitations 
and that U.S. Bank National lacked standing. 
{¶7} On May 19, 2025, Shaffer filed a motion for leave to file a counterclaim. U.S. 
Bank National opposed the motion. 
{¶8} On August 7, 2025, the trial court denied Shaffer’s motion to amend her 
answer to include additional counterclaims. The trial court also granted in part and denied 
in part, U.S. Bank National’s motion for summary judgment and denied Shaffer and

[T]here is some disagreement among courts as to whether 
expiration of the six -year statute of limitations found in R.C. 
1303.16(A) applies to preclude foreclosure under a note. 
However, this Court believes the more reasonable approach 
is to honor the twenty -one-year statute of limitations for 
foreclosure on mortgages as contained in R.C. 2305.04. . . . 

Consequently, the Bank's [motion for summary judgment] is 
DENIED for being time -barred relative to claims for amounts 
owed under the Note. However, the Bank's [motion for 
summary judgment] is GRANTED with respect to its claim for 
foreclosure under the Mortgage. 

{¶9} Additionally, the trial court granted U.S. Bank National’s motion for default 
as to the parties that failed to timely answer or otherwise respond to the complaint. On 
August 8, 2025, Shaffer filed a motion for reconsideration.2 
{¶10} On August 11, 2025, the trial court filed its Judgment Entry and Foreclosure

[O]n the evidence adduced that there is due to [U.S. Bank 
National] on the promissory note set forth in the First Count of 
the Complaint (the "Note"), the sum of $142,118.85 plus 
interest at 6.6500% per annum from March 1, 2018, for which

sum judgment is rendered, in rem, in favor of [U.S.] Bank 
National. 

. . . 

The Court further finds that the conditions in the Mortgage 
have been broken and the same has become absolute and

Premises foreclosed. 

{¶11} The trial court’s entry further determined: 
While finding that there is no just reason for delay as to the 
Plaintiff's claim, the Judge makes no finding at this time as to 
the claims, rights, titles, interests or liens of the Defendants 
LCE Federal Credit Union and John Carroll University as set 
forth in their pleadings filed herein, except to note that such

{¶12} On September 9, 2025, Shaffer filed a pro se motion for relief from judgment 
requesting that the trial court grant her motion for summary judgment and her motion for 
for leave to file a counterclaim, and to dismiss the complaint.3 Additionally, Shaffer filed a
