leads.caseName: Mahmoud Salha and Ali Cafe v. 2020 Harwin 59 Shopping Centers. Ltd., Harwin Exchange Center, Inc., and Mohamed A. Sohani
leads.text:
Opinion issued October 16, 2026 

In The 
Court of Appeals 
For The 
First District of Texas 
———————————— 
NO. 01-25-00652-CV 
——————————— 
MAHMOUD SALHA AND ABU ALI CAFE, Appellants 
V. 
2020 HARWIN 59 SHOPPING CENTERS, LTD., HARWIN EXCHANGE 
CENTER, INC., AND MOHAMED A. SOHANI, Appellees 

On Appeal from the 80th District Court 
Harris County, Texas 
Trial Court Case No. 2022-47567 

MEMORANDUM OPINION 
The appellants, Mahmoud Salha and Abu Ali Café, LLC, sued the appellees, 
2020 Harwin 59 Shopping Centers, Ltd., Harwin Exchange Center, Inc., and 
Mohamed Sohani for breach of contract, fraud, violations of the Deceptive Trade 

2 

Practices Act (DTPA), and relief in quantum meruit for alleged promises concerning 
repairs and consent to sublease. 
In five issues, the appellants contend that the trial court erred in granting 
summary judgment in favor of the appellees and in awarding them their attorney’s 
fees. 
We affirm. 
Background 
On October 1, 2019, Salha and Café Dalida, Inc., executed a commercial lease 
with Harwin Exchange, acting through Sohani, its president, for a restaurant space 
on Richmond Avenue in Houston. The lease had a five-year term. The parties used 
a form promulgated by the Texas Association of Realtors to draft the lease. 
Lease provisions 
Pertinent to this appeal, the lease divides the responsibilities for and costs of 
repair and maintenance of the leased premises between the tenant and landlord. The 
landlord is responsible for roof repairs. If a roof repair is needed, “Tenant must 
promptly notify Landlord . . . in writing.” 
The tenant is responsible for “g rounds maintenance, including landscaping 
and irrigation systems,” “parking areas and walks,” “[p]lumbing systems, drainage 
systems and sump pumps,” and “Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning (HVAC) 
3 

systems.” The tenant is also “ required to maintain, at its expense, a regularly 
scheduled maintenance and service contract for the HVAC system.” 
The lease allows the landlord to “assign this lease to any subsequent owner of 
the [p]roperty.” The tenant, though, “may not assign this lease or sublet any part of 
the leased premises without Landlord ’s written consent”; any attempt to do so “ is 
voidable by Landlord.” And “regardless if the assignment or sublease is made with 
or without the consent of Landlord,” the “ Tenant will remain liable for all of 
Tenant’s obligations under this lease.” 
As for the property ’s condition on move -in, the tenant agrees that he “has 
inspected the leased premises and accepts it in its present (as -is) condition unless 
expressly noted otherwise in this lease or in an addendum.” The landlord “made no 
express or implied warranties as to the condition or permitted use of the leased 
premises or [p]roperty.” 
In a lawsuit between parties to the lease, “[a]ny person who is a prevailing 
party in any legal proceeding brought under or related to the transaction described 
in this lease is entitled to recover prejudgment interest, reasonable attorney’s fees, 
and all other costs of litigation from the nonprevailing party.” 
The lease also provides that it “contains the entire agreement between 
Landlord and Tenant and may not be changed except by written agreement.” 

4 

The parties’ dispute and proceedings below 
The appellants sued the appellees for breach of the lease, fraud, and violation 
of the DTPA. They also sought relief in quantum meruit. In their live pleading, the 
appellants complained that Sohani and Harwin Exchange did not notify them that 
the lease had been assigned to 2020 Harwin in January 2021 and that the appellees 
violated the lease by refusing to maintain or make improvements to the premises. 
Instead, the appellants spent hundreds of thousands of dollars to do so , yet the 
appellees refused to reimburse them. 
According to the appellants, Sohani also enticed them into making substantial 
improvements to the leased premises by promising them that the y would have the 
right to sell their business and that he would approve a sublease. The appellants 
located a buyer for their business and pursued a sublease. As a condition for 
procuring Sohani ’s consent to the sublease, the appellants executed an estoppel 
certificate in which they attested that the landlord was “[not] in default of the lease” 
and they “accepted the leased premises.” Ultimately, though, the appellees refused 
to consent to the sublease. 
After the sublease was rejected, the appellants notified their vendors and 
contractors that the appellees were unwilling to pay for the improvements and a 
materialmen’s lien was placed on the property. 
5 

After substantial discovery, the appellees moved for summary judgment on 
both no-evidence and traditional grounds. The grounds included: (1) recovery under 
quantum meruit was not available for matters covered by the lease; (2) the appellants 
were not entitled to recover their repair expenses under the lease terms; (3) the statute 
of frauds barred recovery on the oral promises they alleged; (4) the appellants were 
not entitled to recover on their fraud claim because they failed to replead it after the 
trial court granted the appellees’ special exceptions; and (5) the appellants’ DTPA 
claim failed because the DTPA did not apply to the lease transaction. The appellees 
also sought to recover their attorney’s fees. 
In its order granting the summary judgment motion, t he trial court specified 
the grounds on which it dismissed the appellants’ claims. The trial court then held a 
hearing on the attorney ’s fee request. The trial court ’s final judgment awarded 
$23,580 for attorney’s fees incurred in the trial court and $15,000 for attorney’s fees 
on appeal. 
Summary Judgment 
A. Standard of Review 
“We review a trial court’s order granting summary judgment de novo, taking 
as true all evidence favorable to the nonmovant, and indulging every reasonable 
inference and resolving any doubts in the nonmovant’s favor.” Cmty. Health Sys. 
Prof’l Servs. v. Hansen, 525 S.W.3d 671, 680 (Tex. 2017) (cleaned up). 
6 

The appellees filed a hybrid no -evidence and traditional summary-judgment 
motion. A no -evidence summary judgment motion shifts the burden to the 
nonmovant to produce evidence raising an issue of material fact as to the elements 
specified in the motion. Mack Trucks, Inc. v. Tamez , 206 S.W.3d 572, 582 (Tex. 
2006). 
To prevail on a traditional motion for summary judgment, “the movant must 
show that no genuine issue of material fact exists and that it is entitled to judgment 
as a matter of law.” Hansen, 525 S.W.3d at 681. A defendant -movant must either 
disprove at least one necessary element of the plaintiff’s theory of recovery or plead 
and conclusively establish each essential element of an affirmative defense. 
Richardson-Eagle, Inc. v. William M. Mercer, Inc. , 213 S.W.3d 469, 473 (Tex. 
App.—Houston [1st Dist.] 2006, pet. denied). Once the movant proves its right to 
judgment as a matter of law, the burden shifts to the nonmovant to present evidence 
raising a fact issue to defeat summary judgment. Id. 
Where, as here, the trial court’s order specifies the grounds on which summary 
judgment was granted , we generally limit our review to those grounds.1 W. Loop 
Hosp., LLC v. Houston Galleria Lodging Assocs., LLC, 649 S.W.3d 461, 480 (Tex. 

1 The trial court recited numerous grounds in its order. We refer only to those 
necessary to adjudicate the appeal. See TEX. R. APP. P. 47.1. 
7 

App.—Houston [1st Dist.] 2022, pet. denied); see Cincinnati Life Ins. Co. v. Cates, 
927 S.W.2d 623, 625–26 (Tex. 1996). 
B. Discussion 
1. Breach of lease 
In their first issue, the appellants assert that the appellees were not entitled to 
summary judgment on the appellants’ claim that the appellees breached the lease’s 
requirement that the landlord fix the electrical panel and wiring, plumbing, air 
conditioning and roof repairs. 
An action for breach of contract requires the plaintiff to prove : (1) an 
enforceable contract exists; (2) the plaintiff performed or tendered performance; 
(3) the defendant breached the contract; and (4) the defendant ’s breach caused the 
plaintiff damages. See USAA Tex. Lloyds Co. v. Menchaca , 545 S.W.3d 479, 501 
n.21 (Tex. 2018). 
In its order granting summary judgment, the trial court dismissed the breach 
of contract claims for repairs to the premises ’ electrical system, plumbing, and air 
conditioning “because maintenance and repair of those systems are assigned to the 
Tenant by the terms of the Lease.” The lease provides that “Tenant will pay for the 
HVAC services under this lease.” The lease defines “HVAC services” as “heating, 
ventilating, and air conditioning of this lease premises.” The lease also designates 
the tenant as responsible for maintaining and repairing plumbing and electrical 
8 

systems. The appellants do not confront this ground for dismissal or address the 
applicable lease terms. 
The lease makes the landlord responsible for roof repairs. If repairs are needed 
that are the landlord ’s responsibility to repair , the lease requires that “Tenant 
promptly notify Landlord” in writing of the need for repair. The trial court 
determined, and the record shows, that there “is no evidence that Plaintiffs gave the 
Landlord a written request for repair of the roof as the Lease requires .” The 
appellants complain that the landlord refused to reimburse them for roof repairs, but 
the lease contains no provision imposing any reimbursement obligation on the 
landlord. And to the extent the appellants asserts that the landlord had an obligation 
to repair the roof before they moved into the leased premises, the lease expressly 
belies that assertion, stating that the tenant “accepts it in its present (as-is) condition.” 
The appellants make no viable argument challenging the trial court’s reasons 
for dismissing these breach-of-contract claims. We overrule their first issue. 
2. Refusal to consent to the sublease 
In their second issue, the appellants assert that the appellees failed to comply 
with their oral agreement requiring them to consent to the sublease. The trial court 
dismissed this claim “as being prohibited by the Statute of Frauds.” 
The record shows that the proposed sublease was to begin January 1, 2018 
and end January 31, 2020. A lease of real estate for a term longer than one year is 
9 

subject to the statute of frauds and is required by law to be in writing. TEX. BUS. & 
COM. CODE § 26.01(a) (1), (b)(5). Thus, the trial court correctly concluded that any 
oral agreement to the sublease was unenforceable. 
We overrule the appellants’ second issue. 
3. DTPA and fraud claims 
In their third issue, the appellants maintain that the trial court erred in granting 
summary judgment dismissing their DTPA and fraud claims. 
The elements of a DTPA claim are: (1) the plaintiff was a consumer; (2) the 
defendant violated a specific provision of the DTPA; and (3) the violation was a 
producing cause of the plaintiff ’s injury. Amstadt v. U.S. Brass Corp. ,919 S.W.2d 
644, 649 (Tex. 1996); see TEX. BUS. & COM. CODE § 17.50(a). 
The DTPA does not apply to a claim that arises from a transaction or set of 
transactions relating to the same nonresidential project if the total consideration by 
the consumer amounts to more than $500,000. See TEX. BUS. & COM. CODE 
§ 17.49(g); AES Valves, LLC v. Kobi Int ’l, Inc., No. 01-18-00081-CV, 2020 WL 
1880781, at *5 (Tex. App.—Houston [1st Dist.] Apr. 16, 2020, pet. denied) (mem. 
op.). Among other reasons for dismissing appellants ’ DTPA claim, the trial court 
determined that dismissal was appropriate because the DTPA did “not apply to the 
Lease transaction whose consideration totals more than $500,000.” 
10 

The lease provides for an initial 60 -month term with “base monthly rent” of 
$8,700 to be paid by the tenant, for a total of $522,000. The appellants assert that the 
“base rent” figure used by the tria

leads.text:
2026 IL App (4th) 260216-U 

NO. 4-26-0216 

IN THE APPELLATE COURT 

OF ILLINOIS 

FOURTH DISTRICT 

LIVINGSTON COUNTY, ILLINOIS, 
 Plaintiff-Appellee, 
 v. 
BRENDA MORRIS, 
 Defendant-Appellant. 

) 
) 
) 
) 
)
) 
)
) 
Appeal from the 
Circuit Court of 
Livingston County 
No. 22OV12 

Honorable 
Mary E. Koll, 
Judge Presiding. 

 JUSTICE LANNERD delivered the judgment of the court. 
 Justices Vancil and Harris concurred in the judgment. 

ORDER 

¶ 1 Held: Defendant’s appeal was dismissed because of h er failure to comply with Illinois 
Supreme Court Rule 341(h) (eff. Oct. 1, 2020). 

¶ 2 Defendant, Brenda Morris, appearing pro se, appeals from a trial court order 
allowing plaintiff, Livingston County, Illinois, to enter her property and remove personal property 
for purposes of bringing it into compliance with a local zoning ordinance prohibiting junkyards. 
Because of the deficiencies of defendant ’s appellant’s brief, we strike her brief and dismiss the 
appeal. 
¶ 3 I. BACKGROUND 
¶ 4 In February 2022, plaintiff filed a complaint alleging defendant violated a zoning 
ordinance by operating a junkyard, which was a nonconforming use of her property. In July 2023, 
the trial court found the property was nonconforming and ordered defendant to bring the property 
FILED 
October 16, 2026 
Carla Bender 
4th District Appellate 
Court, IL 
NOTICE 
This Order was filed under 
Supreme Court Rule 23 and is 
not precedent except in the 
limited circumstances allowed 
under Rule 23(e)(1). 
- 2 - 
into compliance. The record shows multiple subsequent orders requiring defendant to bring the 
property into compliance. Meanwhile, defendant filed multiple motions challenging the initial 
order finding noncompliance, all of which were denied. In March 2024, the court adjudicated 
defendant in contempt . T he record indicates that defendant served time in jail as a contempt 
sanction and did not purge the contempt. 
¶ 5 In December 2024, plaintiff sought an order allowing it to enter the property and 
allow two businesses to provide estimates of the cost of bringing the property into compliance. 
The trial court granted the motion, and defendant appealed. We dismissed the appeal because 
defendant failed to comply with Illinois Supreme Court Rule 341(h) (eff. Oct. 1, 2020). Livingston 
County v. Morris, 2025 IL App (4th) 250040-U, ¶ 16. 
¶ 6 Following the appeal, the trial court held a compliance review, determined 
defendant had not brought the property into compliance, and allowed plaintiff to enter the property 
to inspect it and obtain estimates of the cost of bringing the property into compliance. On January 
16, 2026, the court entered an order following a hearing in which the court “ heard the evidence 
consisting of testimony[ and] the admitted exhibits of the Plaintiff.” The court found the inspection 
had not occurred, but plaintiff was willing to hire third parties to remove any personal property 
necessary to bring the property into compliance. The court authorized plaintiff to do so. The court 
vacated an order imposing periodic imprisonment on defendant. Defendant filed a motion to s tay 
the proceedings, which was denied. There are no transcripts of the hearings in this case in the 
record. However, there are numerous exhibits , including photographs of the property, which 
clearly support a finding it was used as a junkyard. 
¶ 7 This appeal followed. Defendant filed a bystander’s report in the trial court. 
However, the record does not show the report was served on plaintiff or certified by the court. The 
- 3 - 
bystander’s report also does not include facts concerning evidence provided regarding the merits 
of the case. 
¶ 8 II. ANALYSIS 
¶ 9 On appeal, defendant raises issues of due process, excessive fines, unreasonable 
search and seizure, unauthorized prosecution, judicial bias , and service of process . However, 
because defendant’s appellant’s brief fails to comply with multiple paragraphs of Illinois Supreme 
Court Rule 341 (eff. Oct. 1, 2020), which governs the form of appellate briefs , we dismiss the 
appeal. 
¶ 10 At the outset, we note plaintiff has not submitted an appellee’s brief in this appeal. 
However, because we find the record in this case is simple and the issues can be easily decided 
without the aid of an appellee’s brief, we will not reverse on that basis. See First Capitol Mortgage 
Corp. v. Talandis Construction Corp., 63 Ill. 2d 128, 133 (1976). This is especially the case where, 
as here, we dismiss the appeal for failure to comply with Rule 341. See Hamberlin v. Flemming, 
2025 IL App (4th) 241102-U, ¶¶ 14-15. 
¶ 11 This court has the discretion to strike an appellant ’s brief and dismiss an appeal 
when the appellant’s brief does not comply with the requirements of Rule 341. Litwin v. County 
of La Salle, 2021 IL App (3d) 200410, ¶ 11. This is a harsh but appropriate sanction when the 
appellant’s violations of procedural rules hinder our review of the case. Id. 
¶ 12 We recognize defendant is appearing pro se. However, Illinois courts treat pro se 
litigants the same as licensed attorneys. A pro se litigant must comply with the same rules and is 
held to the same standard as a licensed attorney. Holzrichter v. Yorath, 2013 IL App (1st) 110287, 
¶ 78. This is true in both the trial court and this court of review. “[T]he procedural rules governing 
the content and form of appellate briefs are mandatory and not suggestions.” Litwin, 2021 IL App 
- 4 - 
(3d) 200410, ¶ 3. A pro se appellant is not excused from following the requirements of Rule 341. 
Id. 
¶ 13 “Failure to comply with the rules regarding [ appellate] briefs is not an 
inconsequential matter.” Burmac Metal Finishing Co. v. West Bend Mutual Insurance Co., 356 Ill. 
App. 3d 471, 478 (2005). The purpose of the rules is to require parties before a reviewing court to 
present clear and orderly arguments so the court can properly ascertain and dispose of the issues 
involved. Zadrozny v. City Colleges of Chicago, 220 Ill. App. 3d 290, 292 (1991). A brief that 
lacks any substantial conformity to the rules may justifiably be stricken. Tannenbaum v. Lincoln 
National Bank, 143 Ill. App. 3d 572, 574 (1986). 
¶ 14 Defendant’s appellate brief violates multiple rules that govern appeals. In 
particular, Rule 341(h)(6) requires an appellant’s brief to contain a statement of the facts necessary 
to an understanding of the case, stated fairly and without argument or comment, and with 
appropriate citations to the record on appeal. Ill. S. Ct. R . 341(h)(6) (eff. Oct. 1, 2020). “A 
reviewing court is not obligated to search the record for evidence on which to base a reversal, and 
unless reference is made to those portions of the record supporting reversal, the argument will not 
be considered.” Webb v. Angell, 155 Ill. App. 3d 848, 854 (1987). 
¶ 15 Here, defendant provides brief paragraphs of procedural facts with brackets and 
blank lines inserted, indicating an intent to insert citations to the recor d. However, no actual 
citations are given. In addition, no facts pertaining to the merits are given, despite a hearing having 
been held where testimony was provided and photographs admitted into evidence depicting the 
property as junkyard. 
¶ 16 Further, Rule 341(h)(7) requires the brief to contain an argument section, “which 
shall contain the contentions of the appellant and the reasons therefor, with citation of the 
- 5 - 
authorities and the pages of the record relied on.” Ill. S. Ct. R. 341(h)(7) (eff. Oct. 1, 2020). An 
appellant is obligated to define issues clearly, cite pertinent authority, and present a cohesive legal 
argument. Gandy v. Kimbrough, 406 Ill. App. 3d 867, 875 (2010). Moreover, defendant does not 
assert that her failure to cite pertinent authority is the result of her claims being matters of first 
impression or novel in nature. Moreover, in much the same manner that this court is not obligated 
to search the record to find reasons to reverse the trial court ’s judgment, this court is also not a 
depository into which an appellant may dump the burden of research and argument with regard to 
the issues he or she raises on appeal. In re Marriage of Hundley, 2019 IL App (4th) 180380, ¶ 82. 
Instead, this court is “entitled to have the issues clearly defined and a cohesive legal argument 
presented.” Id. Contentions that are inadequately presented on appeal, such as by the failure to 
provide coherent argument or cite pertinent authority, do not merit consideration. Holmstrom v. 
Kunis, 221 Ill. App. 3d 317, 325 (1991). 
¶ 17 Defendant’s legal contentions generally consist of short paragraphs stating a 
boilerplate proposition of law and a conclusory assertion of error. D efendant routinely provides 
broad legal principles without a cogent explanation of their relevance or how they apply to the 
facts of her case. Nothing is applied to facts elicited at hearings regarding the merits of the case. 
¶ 18 As an example, defendant asserts the trial court imposed excessive fines and 
enforcement measures that were grossly disproportionate to the alleged zoning violation. However, 
she does not provide facts and analysis concerning the merits of the court’s findings regarding any 
fines, any enforcement measures, or the severity of the zoning violation. Instead, she merely states 
without meaningful analysis that the enforcement measures were unconstitutional . Defendant’s 
other arguments suffer from the same deficiencies. 
¶ 19 Defendant’s lack of a complete statement of facts concerning the merits of the 
- 6 - 
issues presented for review, coupled with her lack of substantive legal arguments, results in an 
inability to address her issues on appeal. Overall, defendant failed to provide any cogent or 
meaningful legal analysis. Accordingly, we dismiss the appeal. 
¶ 20 We also note, even if we were to excuse the shortcomings of defendant’s brief, we 
would then affirm based on the lack of a report of proceedings. 
¶ 21 “[A]n appellant has the burden to present a sufficiently complete record of the 
proceedings at trial to support a claim of error, and in the absence of such a record on appeal, it 
will be presumed that the order entered by the trial court was in conformity with law and had a 
sufficient factual basis. Any doubts which may arise from the incompleteness of the record will be 
resolved against the appellant.” Foutch v. O’Bryant, 99 Ill. 2d 389, 391-92 (1984). In the absence 
of a complete record, we must presume that the trial court acted properly. See id. at 392. 
¶ 22 Defendant filed a bystander’s report, which she states in her brief was approved by 
the trial court. However, we are unable to find a certification of the report by the court in the 
documents in the record or the court’s docket entries. Defendant has not provided a citation to the 
location of any such certification in the record. The record also does not contain anything showing 
the report was served on plaintiff. Illinois Supreme Court Rule 323(c) (eff. July 1, 2017) requires 
service on all parties and does not allow an uncertified bystander’s report to be included in the 
record on appeal. Defendant ’s bystander’s report also failed to include facts concerning the 
testimony and evidence presented by the parties concerning the merits of the action. 
¶ 23 Here, we lack a record of the testimony and full extent of the evidence presented at 
the hearings. Thus, were we to consider the merits, we would affirm based on the lack of a 
complete record. 
¶ 24 We recognize the dismissal of an appeal is a harsh sanction. However, because of 
- 7 - 
the deficiencies in defendant’s appellant’s brief, we find the dismissal of her appeal appropriate. 
¶ 25 III. CONCLUSION 
¶ 26 For the foregoing reasons, we strike defendant’s brief and dismiss the appeal. 
¶ 27 Appeal dismissed.

UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS 

FOR THE TENTH CIRCUIT 
_________________________________ 
AUGUST WAKAT, 

 Plaintiff - Appellant, 

and 

POEBOY FLEMING AUTO 
SALVAGE, INC., 

 Plaintiff, 

v. 

CITY OF TULSA; 
JOE ROBSON, individually and as agent 
of Fair Oaks L.L.C.; HENRY WINN; 
LAMAR ADVERTISING CO.; 
PLAINVIEW SALVAGE INC., 

 Defendants - Appellees, 

and 

FAIR OAKS TOWNSHIP; 
ANN LANDRITH TRUST; ROBERT 
RAINBOLT; JEREMY BILLINGSLY; 
JOHN DOE, 9-50, unknown persons 
acting in concert under the moniker 
“Cowboy Mafia”, 

 Defendants. 

No. 25-5114 
(D.C. No. 4:24-CV-00564-JDR-MTS) 
(N.D. Okla.) 
_________________________________ 
ORDER AND JUDGMENT* 

* After examining the briefs and appellate record, this panel has determined 
unanimously that oral argument would not materially assist in the determination of 
this appeal. See Fed. R. App. P. 34(a)(2); 10th Cir. R. 34.1(G). The case is therefore 
FILED 
United States Court of Appeals 
Tenth Circuit 

October 16, 2026 

Christopher M. Wolpert 
Clerk of Court 
Appellate Case: 25-5114 Document: 77-1 Date Filed: 10/16/2026 Page: 1 
2 

_________________________________ 
Before MATHESON, CARSON, and ROSSMAN, Circuit Judges. 
_________________________________ 
Appellant August Wakat owns a parcel of land near Tulsa, Oklahoma. But 
according to him, a vast array of private and state actors —collectively known as the 
“cowboy mafia”— have conspired to dispossess him of the land and prevent him from 
vindicating his property rights in court. 
The district court dismissed Mr. Wakat’s complaint for failure to state a claim. 
Mr. Wakat appeals pro se 1 from the dismissal order. We have jurisdiction under 
28 U.S.C. § 1291, and we affirm. Both in the district court and on appeal, Mr. Wakat 
has waived his challenges to each defendant’s dismissal from the action. 
BACKGROUND 
The operative complaint alleges that Henry Winn conveyed a parcel of land to 
Mr. Wakat by general warranty deed. Unbeknownst to Mr. Wakat, the title was 
encumbered by defendants’ various “conflicting and adverse claims ” on the property. 
Suppl. R. vol. 2 at 16 ¶ 112. For instance, Mr. Winn had previously erected several 

ordered submitted without oral argument. This order and judgment is not binding 
precedent, except under the doctrines of law of the case, res judicata, and collateral 
estoppel. It may be cited, however, for its persuasive value consistent with 
Fed. R. App. P. 32.1 and 10th Cir. R. 32.1 . 
1 We will construe a pro se litigant’s papers liberally, but we will not “serv[e] 
as the litigant’s attorney in constructing arguments and searching the record.” 
Garrett v. Selby Connor Maddux & Janer , 425 F.3d 836, 840 (10th Cir. 2005). We 
will also hold the pro se litigant to “the same rules of procedure that govern other 
litigants.” Id. (internal quotation marks omitted). 
Appellate Case: 25-5114 Document: 77-1 Date Filed: 10/16/2026 Page: 2 
3 

structures on the land , including a billboard installed by Lamar Advertising . These 
structures violated zoning ordinances and had to be professionally remov ed, causing 
a $12 million mechanic’s lien on the property. Relatedly , in what Mr. Wakat calls a 
“21st Century Land Heist,” the City of Tulsa had previously annexed the parcel 
without due process. Id. at 47. This unlawful annexation enabled the city to assess 
fines of $1,200 per day for the above ordinance violations . Mr. Wakat has been 
harmed financially by these clouds on his land title, including having to close his 
business, being haled into sham foreclosure proceedings, and losing a $15 million 
land sale contract . 
The complaint alleges that defendants have conspired with public officials —
all as part of the “cowboy mafia” led by Joe Robson —to deprive Mr. Wakat of his 
property without due process . See id. at 6 ¶ 33; 16 ¶ 112. It alleges further that the 
cowboy mafia’s influence has rendered him “unable to obtain a fair and impartial 
tribunal hearing due to systemic bias.” Id. at 7 ¶ 38. He asserts claims for relief 
under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, declaratory judgment, and quiet title under Oklahoma law. 
In the district court , four of the named defendants 2—the City of Tulsa, Joe 
Robson, Henry Winn, and Lamar Advertising— each moved to dismiss the complaint 
for failure to state a claim. Mr. Wakat filed a response in opposition to Mr. Robson’s 

2 The operative complaint also named five other defendants —Fair Oaks 
Township, Ann Landrith Trust, Robert Rainbolt, Jeremy Billingsly, and Plainview 
Salvage, Inc. —who were dismissed from the action as never properly served. See R. 
vol. 1 at 90 & n.4. Similarly, the corporate plaintiff, Poeboy Fleming Auto Salvage, 
Inc., was dismissed after no counsel appeared on its behalf. Id. at 89 & n.1. 
Appellate Case: 25-5114 Document: 77-1 Date Filed: 10/16/2026 Page: 3 
4 

motion. See Suppl. R. vol. 6 at 7 –11. But he did not do the same for the other three 
motions to dismiss —instead, he objected and moved to strike those filings as 
improperly successive. See id. at 74–78. 
Upon review of the complaint, t he district court granted all four motions to 
dismiss in a single order. This appeal timely followed. 
DISCUSSION 
Mr. Wakat seeks to challenge the dismissal of his complaint for failure to state 
a claim . But at various stages of the litigation, he has waived or abandoned his 
arguments as to each defendant ’s dismissal from the action . 
Consider Mr. Robson first. The district court recounted the complaint’s 
allegations that he (i) tried to initiate a “land swap” with Mr. Wakat, (ii) refused to 
testify in another case regarding Mr. Wakat’s land dispute, (iii) influenced 
Mr. Wakat’s lawsuit s as a member of Oklahoma’s judicial nominati ng committee, 
and (iv) was involved in the city’s code enforcement operations against Mr. Wakat. 
It then concluded the complaint failed to allege that Mr. Robson conspired with 
government officials to violate Mr. Wakat’s constitutional rights. 
Mr. Wakat does not meaningfully dispute this reasoning on appeal. Indeed, 
his entire analysis of Mr. Robson’s alleged role in the conspiracy is limited to just 
one sentence , where he argues that Robson’s and other defendants’ “conduct is 
plausibly ‘state action’ at the pleading stage because [they] allegedly acted jointly 
with City officials and used governmental authority to effect the deprivation.” Aplt. 
Br. at 10. This will not do. Although we construe Mr. Wakat’s briefing liberally, he 
Appellate Case: 25-5114 Document: 77-1 Date Filed: 10/16/2026 Page: 4 
5 

was still required at a minimum “to explain to us why the district court’s decision 
was wrong. ” Nixon v. City & Cnty. of Denver , 784 F.3d 1364, 1366 (10th Cir. 2015). 
And here, this single sentence in the opening brief, unaccompanied by any effort at 
developed argument, is woefully insufficient to challenge the district court’s reasons 
for dismissing Mr. Robson from the action. See, e.g. , Murrell v. Shalala , 43 F.3d 
1388, 1389 n.2 (10th Cir.1994) (“a few scattered” and “perfunctory” statements that 
fail to frame and develop an issue are insufficient appellate argument ); see also Fed. 
R. App. P. 28(a)(8). Accordingly, we deem Mr. Wakat’s arguments as to 
Mr. Robson ’s dismissal below waived and decline to consider them . See In re 
Syngenta AG MIR 162 Corn Litig. , 61 F.4th 1126, 1181 (10th Cir. 2023) (a litigant 
“may waive appellate review of an issue by not arguing it —or arguing it in an 
inadequate manner— in [his] opening brief”) ; Toevs v. Reid , 685 F.3d 903, 911 
(10th Cir. 20 12) (“Arguments not clearly made in a party’s opening brief are deemed 
waived.”). 
This appellate- briefing waiver applies in equal measure for the other three 
defendants . As to Lamar Advertising, the complaint had alleged that there was a 
mechanic’s lien on the property because of a nonconforming billboard; in the district 
court’s view, this was insufficient to allege Lamar Advertising’s engagement in state 
action for § 1983 purposes. On appeal, Mr. Wakat’s opening brief devotes roughly 
half a page to challenging Lamar Advertising ’s dismissal from the action. See Aplt. 
Br. at 13. This section contains no discussion of the applicable standard of review, 
and no citation to where, if at all, this argument was raised before the district court ; 
Appellate Case: 25-5114 Document: 77-1 Date Filed: 10/16/2026 Page: 5 
6 

instead, it consists largely of citations to various legal authoritie s without further 
explanation . See id. This does not suffice to invoke our review. 
The same goes for the City of Tulsa’s dismissal . The district court reasoned 
that the complaint had not tied any official policy or custom to Mr. Wakat’s harm for 
Monell purposes; instead, it alleged that various individuals affiliated with the city 
had used ordinance violations on the property to impose fines. But as before, the 
opening brief’s challeng e to the city’s dismissal is limited to roughly one page, 
without any reference to the applicable standard of review, record citations, or 
developed explanation of the district court ’s error. See Aplt. Br. at 11–12. Again, 
this is insufficient appellate argument. 
So, too, for Mr. Winn’s dismissal. T he complaint alleges that Mr. Winn 
conveyed a general warranty deed to Mr. Wakat but failed to deliver clear title 
because of the ordinance violations and mechanic’s lien; here again, the district court 
concluded that these allegations did not amount to engagement in state action for 
§ 1983 purposes. But the opening brief’s treatment of Mr. Winn’s dismissal is 
similarly limited to “a few scattered” and “perfunctory” statements about his state-
law quiet title claim , devoid of citations to the record or legal authorit ies, nor any 
meaningful explanation of how the district court erred. See id. at 11, 14, 16 –17; see 
also Murrell, 43 F.3d at 1389 n.2 . As before, this is inadequate presentation. 
From the foregoing, this much is clear— Mr. Wakat’s cursory arguments as to 
the dismissals of Lamar Advertising, the City of Tulsa, and Mr. Winn are 
insufficiently briefed on appeal and therefore waived. See In re Syngenta AG 
Appellate Case: 25-5114 Document: 77-1 Date Filed: 10/16/2026 Page: 6 
7 

MIR 162 Corn Litig. , 61 F.4th at 1181 ; Toevs, 685 F.3d at 911 ; see also Fed. R. App. 
P. 28(a)(8). 
There is more. Mr. Wakat’s arguments regarding these three defendants suffer 
from an additional waiver problem —he never made them in the district court , and he 
does not make any plain -error arguments now, precluding appellate review. “When a 
party fails to raise an argument below, we typically treat the argument as forfeited.” 
United States v. Leffler , 942 F.3d 1192, 1196 (10th Cir. 2019). “And when an 
appellant raises a forfeited argument on appeal, we will reverse only if the appellant 
can satisfy our rigorous plain -error test.” Id. However, if the appellant “fails to 
preserve an issue and also fails to make a plain -error argument on appeal, we 
ordinarily deem the issue waived (rather than merely forfeited) and decline to review 
the issue at all —for plain error or otherwise.” Id. 
Here, Mr. Wakat’s opposition to the dismissals of Lamar Advertising, the 
City of Tulsa, and Mr. Winn comes too late. Although he objected and moved to 
strike their motions to dismiss as improperly successive,
3 he did not file any 
substantive response to them. See Suppl. R. vol. 6 at 74 –78. So, t he district court 
never passed upon many of the arguments he makes now— including, for instance, his 

3 Contrary to Mr. Wakat’s suggestion, these motions to dismiss the operative 
complaint were not improperly duplicative or successive. Each of the four 
defendants moved to dismiss Mr. Wakat’s initial complaint. But before the district 
court ruled on them, Mr. Wakat amended his complaint, thereby mooting the four 
motions. See Suppl. R. vol. 6 at 5 –6. Thereafter, the four defendants renewed their 
motions in response to th

[Cite as Union Home Mtge. Corp. v. Hinds, 2026-Ohio-4082.] 

IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF OHIO 
SIXTH APPELLATE DISTRICT 
LUCAS COUNTY 

Union Home Mortgage, et al. 

 Appellees 

v. 

Lauren Hinds, et al. 

 Appellant 
Court of Appeals No. L-25-00273 

Trial Court No. CI0202302986 

DECISION AND JUDGMENT 

Decided: October 16, 2026 

* * * * * 

Mia L. Conner, for appellee, Union Home Mortgage Corp. 

Brady J. Lighthall, for appellee, The Huntington National Bank. 

Beau Harvey, pro se, appellant. 

* * * * * 
SULEK, J. 
{¶ 1} Appellant, Beau Harvey, pro se, appeals the November 20, 2024 judgments 
of the Lucas County Court of Common Pleas which (1) granted appellee Union Home 
Mortgage Corporation summary judgment on its foreclosure claim and dismissed the 
counterclaim of defendant Lauren Hinds and granted judgment on the pleadings as to 

2. 

Harvey and (2) granted appellee Huntington National Bank default judgment on its cross-
claim against Hinds and Harvey. The court then entered a foreclosure decree as to both 
Harvey and Hinds as co-tenants with survivorship rights, and ordered the sale of the 
property. Because the record fails to establish that Union Home perfected service of 
process as to Harvey and that Harvey did not waive the defect, the judgment is reversed, 
in part, and remanded to the trial court for further proceedings 
I. Factual and Procedural Background 
{¶ 2} In August 2013, Lauren Hinds, unmarried, executed a promissory note for 
$136,704 which was secured by a mortgage on real property located on Timothy Lane in 
Sylvania, Lucas County, Ohio. Harvey and Hinds became joint tenants of the property 
with survivorship rights by deed recorded on March 31, 2017. In June 2023, Union 
Home became the holder of the note. In 2018, Hinds entered into a personal credit line 
agreement with Huntington, with a $71,700 limit, which was secured by a mortgage on 
the Timothy Lane property and signed by Hinds and Harvey. 
{¶ 3} On July 7, 2023, Union Home filed a complaint in foreclosure and an 
amended complaint on July 10. The complaint named Hinds and Harvey as titleholders 
of the property as well as various lienholders, including Huntington. 
{¶ 4} Union Home attempted service of the complaint and amended complaint by 
certified mail. As to Harvey, there is no evidence in the record, by return of service or 
otherwise, that Union Home properly served him in accordance with Civ.R. 3(A). 
{¶ 5} On September 13, 2023, Hinds filed an answer, asserted fraud and breach of 
contract counterclaims, and moved to dismiss under Civ.R. 12(B)(6) for failure to state a 

3. 

claim. Harvey filed no answer, no motion under Civ.R. 12, and no other responsive 
pleading. He raised no objection to service at any time prior to the foreclosure judgment. 
{¶ 6} Huntington filed an answer and cross-claim against Hinds and Harvey 
claiming that it held a note with a principal of $71,339.11, which was in default and that 
it was secured by a valid mortgage on the property. Huntington requested that the 
mortgage be foreclosed on and that the note be repaid. The record evidences that 
Huntington served the cross-claim on Harvey and Hinds by certified mail on January 19, 
2024. 
{¶ 7} On January 30, 2024, the parties participated in court-ordered telephonic 
mediation, with Hinds and Harvey appearing pro se. The magistrate’s report reflects that 
following discussions, Hinds and Harvey agreed to complete and return a loss mitigation 
packet and Union Home’s counsel would provide reinstatement figures. On March 1, 
2024, the magistrate entered a final mediation report stating that “based on the 
information received from Defendant Beau Harvey, mediation is hereby 
TERMINATED.” 
{¶ 8} On March 22, 2024, Union Home moved for summary judgment on its 
amended complaint and on Hinds’ counterclaim. In a separate filing, Union Home 
moved for judgment on the pleadings as to Harvey and for default judgment as to Capital 
One Bank and Bank of America. On May 2, 2024, Huntington moved for default 
judgment on its cross-claim against Hinds and Harvey. 

4. 

{¶ 9} On September 26, 2024, Judge Mandros requested that the administrative 
judge reassign the matter to another Lucas County judge. The administrative judge 
ultimately assigned the matter to Judge Stacy Cook. 
{¶ 10} In the interim, on November 20, 2024, a visiting judge granted Union 
Home summary judgment on its amended foreclosure complaint and dismissed Hinds’ 
counterclaim. The court first concluded that “all necessary parties have been served with 
Summons according to laws and are properly before the Court.” As to Harvey, it found: 
[B]ased upon the evidence that Defendant Beau Harvey aka Beauregard M. 
Harvey, is in default of Motion or Answer but appeared in a limited 
capacity to participate in court-ordered mediation; based on this limited 
appearance, Plaintiff’s Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings is granted 
against to [sic] Beau Harvey aka Beauregard M. Harvey. 

The court then ordered that the equity of redemption of the property be foreclosed and it 
be sold. 
{¶ 11} In a separate judgment entry, the court granted default judgment on 
Huntington’s cross-claim against Hinds and Harvey finding Hinds in default of the note 
and Huntington entitled to a foreclosure decree on the mortgage. On December 18, 
successor Judge Stacy Cook entered a modified judgment entry and foreclosure decree as 
to Huntington to reflect a recalculation of the debt based on interest rate changes. 
{¶ 12} On January 23, 2025, Harvey filed an affidavit with the Ohio Supreme 
Court seeking to disqualify Judge Dean Mandros from presiding over the matter; the 
Court summarily denied the request as moot, noting that Judge Mandros had already 
recused himself. 

5. 

{¶ 13} Also on January 23, Hinds moved to have the foreclosure judgments 
vacated based on her assertion that Judge Mandros lacked jurisdiction to sign the October 
15, 20241 orders after recusing himself on September 26, 2024. Hinds further claimed 
that Harvey had not been served and that the court failed to follow the scheduling order 
as set forth in the local rules. Harvey similarly moved to vacate the judgments. 
{¶ 14} This appeal followed. 
II. Assignments of Error 
{¶ 15} Harvey raises five assignments of error for review: 
I. The trial court did not have jurisdiction to enter an order of foreclosure 
when there is no service over a defendant within one year pursuant to Civil 
Rule 3(A) rendering all proceedings void ab initio. 

II. The trial court erred by entering orders affecting Beau Harvey’s property 
interest where no service was perfected and no waiver occurred, depriving 
the court of personal jurisdiction and rendering the foreclosure decree void. 

III. The trial court erred as a matter of law in granting summary judgment. 

IV. The foreclosure decree is void because it was entered during a judicial 
reassignment by a visiting judge without lawful authority depriving the trial 
court of the judicial power to enter a final dispositive order. 

V. The proceedings violated appellant’s rights to due process and equal 
protection under the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments to the United States 
Constitution and Article I, Sections 1, 2, and 16 of the Ohio Constitution, 
rendering the foreclosure decree unconstitutional and void. 

1The orders at issue were filed on November 19, 2024, journalized on November 20, and 
signed by a visiting judge. The court docket reflects an October 15, 2024 add date 
though the entries each individually state that they were added on November 19. 

6. 

III. Preliminary Matters 
{¶ 16} Two factors narrow the scope of this appeal. First, Hinds is not a party to 
it. The filing of a notice of appeal in the trial court–Hinds filed none–invokes the 
authority of this court. See R.C. 2505.04. Second, Harvey, who is not an attorney, may 
not represent her. Thus, consideration of Harvey’s arguments on appeal are limited to 
those portions of the judgments directly impacting his interest as a co-tenant of the 
property. 
IV. Analysis 
A. Commencement of the Action 
{¶ 17} Harvey’s first assignment of error, that the entire action be declared void ab 
initio, sweeps too broadly. Under Civ,R. 3(A), “[a] civil action is commenced by filing a 
complaint with the court, if service is obtained within one year from such filing upon a 
named defendant…” (Emphasis added.). The rule “does not require all defendants to 
have been served for a civil action to be considered commenced.” Beneficial Ohio, Inc. 
v. Ellis, 2009-Ohio-311, ¶ 18; see also Fong v. Faires, 2025-Ohio-1032, ¶ 13 (10th 
Dist.). 
{¶ 18} Here, Union Home commenced this civil action when it obtained service 
on a named defendant (i.e., Hinds) within one year of filing the complaint. Thus, the 
judgment entered against co-defendant Hinds who signed and defaulted on the notes, and 
was served, appeared, and litigated is valid. Even if the judgment as to Hinds could be 
considered voidable, she failed to perfect an appeal in this court to challenge the 
judgment. Harvey’s first assignment of error is not well-taken. 

7. 

B. Civ.R. 3(A) Service and Personal Jurisdiction 
{¶ 19} Harvey’s second and fifth assignments of contend that the trial court erred 
by entering orders affecting his property rights where Union Home never served him with 
the foreclosure complaint and, thus, the action was never commenced and was void ab 
initio. Appellate review of a trial court’s decision on personal jurisdiction is de novo as a 
question of law. Universal Acceptance Corp. v. Colbert, 2019-Ohio-4377, ¶ 21 (6th 
Dist.), citing Fraley v. Estate of Oeding, 2014-Ohio-452, ¶ 11. 
{¶ 20} “Service is an essential component of commencing an action under Civ.R. 
3(A) because this is the process through which a court with venue and subject matter 
jurisdiction ‘asserts jurisdiction over the person of the party served.’” Messenger v. 
State, 2020-Ohio-851, ¶ 11(3d Dist.), quoting During v. Quoico, 2012-Ohio-2990, ¶ 25 
(10th Dist.), quoting Mississippi Publishing Corp. v. Murphree, 326 U.S. 438, 444-45 
(1946). 
{¶ 21} “‘Inaction upon the part of a defendant who is not served with process, 
even though he might be aware of the filing of the action, does not dispense with the 
necessity of service.’” Gliozzo v. Univ. Urologists of Cleveland, Inc., 2007-Ohio-3762, ¶ 
16, quoting Maryhew v. Yova, 11 Ohio St.3d 154, 157 (1984). The obligation is upon 
plaintiffs to perfect service of process; defendants have no duty to assist them in fulfilling 
this obligation. Maryhew at 159. 
{¶ 22} When service is not properly made, a trial court lacks jurisdiction over the 
defendant who was not properly served; consequently, any judgment issued against that 
defendant is void. Treasurer of Lucas Cty. v. Mt. Airy Invs. Ltd., 2019-Ohio-3932, ¶ 12 

8. 

(6th Dist.), citing Cavalry Invest., LLC v. Clevenger, 2005-Ohio-7003, ¶ 9 (6th Dist.). 
However, as to the served defendant the judgment may be voidable but must be raised 
either in a motion to vacate or on direct appeal. 
{¶ 23} Because proper service is required under Civ.R. 3(A), Civ.R. 12(H) 
provides the exclusive means by which a party may waive service defects. Ackman v. 
Mercy Heath West Hosp., L.L.C., 2024-Ohio-3159, ¶ 17. The section relevantly 
provides: 
A defense of lack of jurisdiction over the person, . . . insufficiency of 
process, or insufficiency of service of process is waived (A) if omitted from 
a motion in the circumstances described in subdivision (G), or (B) if it is 
neither made by motion under this rule nor included in a responsive 
pleading or an amendment thereof permitted by Rule 15(A) to be made as a 
matter of course. 

{¶ 24} Thus, to render a judgment against a defendant who is not served with 
process, there must be a showing upon the record that the defendant has voluntarily 
submitted himself to the court’s jurisdiction or committed other acts which con

Case: 25-30381 Document: 58-1 Page: 1 Date Filed: 10/16/2026

 United States Court of Appeals
 for the Fifth Circuit United States Court of Appeals
 ____________ Fifth Circuit

 FILED
 No. 25-30381 October 16, 2026
 ____________
 Thomas B. Plunkett, III
 Clerk
Joy Banner, Doctor of Philosophy,

 Plaintiff—Appellant,

 versus

Michael Wright, in his individual and official capacities;
St. John the Baptist Parish;
Jaclyn Hotard, in her individual and official capacities,

 Defendants—Appellees.
 ______________________________

 Appeal from the United States District Court
 for the Eastern District of Louisiana
 USDC No. 2:23-CV-7296
 ______________________________

Before Smith and Higginson, Circuit Judges. *
Per Curiam:
 Joy Banner sued St. John the Baptist Parish and two of its officers for
alleged violations of her rights at a public meeting. A jury returned a verdict
against her on all counts. The district court denied her motion for a new trial.
We vacate and remand for a new trial.

 _____________________
 *
 Judge Wiener was a member of the original panel but did not participate in this
decision. This case is decided by a quorum. See 28 U.S.C. § 46(d).

 1
 Case: 25-30381 Document: 58-1 Page: 2 Date Filed: 10/16/2026

 No. 25-30381

 I.
 The parish regularly elects a suite of officers, including a Parish Presi-
dent and a nine-member Council. On November 28, 2023, the Council con-
vened a meeting led by Parish President Jaclyn Hotard. At some point during
the meeting, Banner stepped to the lectern and declared her intent to com-
ment on Agenda Item J, which concerned an “Authorization to retain Legal
Service with the Law Firm, R. Gray Sexton, as Special Counsel, to perform
services related to Ethics Laws subject to the restrictions imposed by the
State of Louisiana regarding Ethics Procedures and at the rate in accordance
with the Attorney General Guidelines per statute.”
 It is unsurprising that Banner wished to speak on that subject. Not too
long before the meeting, she had filed an ethics complaint against Hotard,
alleging that Hotard had impermissibly participated in an industrial zoning
decision that would directly benefit the financial interests of her immediate
family. At the time, that was the only ethical complaint pending against the
Parish or any of its officers.
 Banner’s remarks at the meeting, however, were short-lived. After
just five seconds, Banner was interrupted, first by Hotard and then by Coun-
cil Chairman Michael Wright. Banner was instructed that her planned dia-
tribe about the pending ethics complaint was off-topic, and she was ordered
to limit the scope of her statements to approved agenda items. Wright then
recited La. Rev. Stat. § 42:1141.4(L)(1), which provides:
 It shall be a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of not more
 than two thousand dollars or imprisonment for not more than
 one year, or both, for any member of the Board of Ethics, its
 executive secretary, other employee, or any other person, other
 than the person who is subject to the investigation or com-
 plaint, to make public the testimony taken at a private investi-
 gation or private hearing of the Board of Ethics or to make any
 public statement or give out any information concerning a pri-

 2
 Case: 25-30381 Document: 58-1 Page: 3 Date Filed: 10/16/2026

 No. 25-30381

 vate investigation or private hearing of the Board of Ethics
 without the written request of the public servant or other per-
 son investigated.
Wright further told Banner to “stop this comment” and that she was “in
violation of state law.” Banner understood the statement as a threat and end-
ed her comment without using the materials she had brought to the lectern
or fully discussing her concerns.
 As it turns out, though, Section 42:1141.4(L)(1) had been ruled uncon-
stitutional nearly a decade earlier. See King v. Caldwell ex rel. La., 21 F. Supp.
3d 651, 656 (E.D. La. 2014). This statute was properly included in the Un-
constitutional Statutes Biennial Report to the Legislature, and the piece of
paper from which Wright read during the meeting was, in fact, marked
“unconstitutional” at the top.
 After discovering the statute’s invalidity, Banner sued Hotard,
Wright, and the Parish under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for First Amendment dis-
crimination and retaliation against protected speech. Banner also brought
state law claims under Louisiana’s Constitution and Open Meetings Law.

 II.
 The jury unanimously found in favor of defendants on all counts.
During the trial, however, counsel for defendants, as the district court
acknowledged, “repeatedly crossed the bounds of proper advocacy.” Coun-
sel ignored the district court’s directives and potentially prejudiced the ver-
dict on dozens of occasions. The district court catalogued this misfeasance
as follows:
 (1) Defense counsel questioned Michael Wright about an
 “email and a phone call from District Attorney Keith Green,”
 despite the exclusion of an advice of counsel defense. Plain-
 tiff’s counsel objected; the Court sustained the objection.

 3
 Case: 25-30381 Document: 58-1 Page: 4 Date Filed: 10/16/2026

 No. 25-30381

 (2) Defense counsel questioned witnesses on their understand-
 ing of the law, despite the Court’s instruction not to do so.
 Plaintiff’s counsel objected; the Court overruled the objection.
 (3) Defense counsel asked witness Guillot about her “legal
 position” despite the Court’s instruction not to do so. Plain-
 tiff’s counsel objected; the Court sustained the objection.
 (4) Defense counsel asked witness Guillot about who the “stat-
 ute applies to” despite the Court’s instruction not to ask legal
 questions. Plaintiff’s counsel objected; the Court sustained the
 objection.
 (5) Defense counsel asked witness Guillot what she “would
 advise” a person, despite the Court’s instruction not to ask
 legal questions. The Court, sua sponte, interjected and stopped
 the line of questioning.
 (6) Defense counsel asked witness Landeche whether St. John
 the Baptist Parish’s actions were “in compliance with the
 Open Meetings Law” despite the Court’s instruction not to
 ask legal questions. Plaintiff’s counsel objected; the Court
 overruled the objection.
 (7) Defense counsel asked witness Landeche about what the
 Open Meetings Law “requires” and whether St. John the Bap-
 tist Parish “complied” with the law despite the Court’s in-
 struction not to ask legal questions.
 (8) Defense counsel asked Michael Wright whether Ms. Per-
 rilloux was “violating any constitutionality statute,” despite
 instructions from the Court not to ask lay witnesses legal ques-
 tions. Plaintiff’s counsel objected; the Court sustained the
 objection.
 (9) Defense counsel questioned witness Guillot about the dis-
 missal of the underlying ethics complaint despite the Court’s
 ruling that said dismissal was “not a material fact in this case.”
 The Court, sua sponte, interjected and stopped the line of
 questioning.

 4
 Case: 25-30381 Document: 58-1 Page: 5 Date Filed: 10/16/2026

 No. 25-30381

 (10) Defense counsel questioned witnesses about the dismissal
 of the underlying ethics complaint despite the Court’s ruling
 that said dismissal was immaterial.
 (11) Defense counsel referenced the dismissal of the underlying
 ethics complaint in closing argument despite the Court’s ruling
 that said dismissal was immaterial.
 (12) Defense counsel questioned witness Sexton about his un-
 derstanding of the meaning of “confidential” despite the
 Court’s ruling not to do so. The Court, sua sponte, interjected
 and stopped the line of questioning.
 (13) Defense counsel described Plaintiff’s public comment as
 “inappropriate” despite the Court’s instruction not to use the
 word as it would suggest the comment was unlawful.
 (14) Defense counsel questioned witness Landry about the in-
 ternal operations of the Board of Ethics despite being in-
 structed not to do so.
 (15) Defense counsel questioned witness Guillot about the
 internal operations of the Board of Ethics despite being in-
 structed not to do so.
 (16) Defense counsel questioned witnesses about “prominent
 supporters” of the underlying industrial project despite in-
 structions not to do so.
 (17) Defense counsel stated in opening argument that Louisi-
 ana Revised Statute § 42:1141.4(L)(1) “is the law” even
 though the statute was ruled unconstitutional nine years prior.
 Plaintiff’s counsel objected. The Court sustained the
 objection.
 (18) Defense counsel stated in opening argument that Plain-
 tiff’s actions were “contrary to the statute” even though the
 statute was ruled unconstitutional. Plaintiff’s counsel objected.
 The objection was sustained, and the jury was instructed to dis-
 regard the statement.
 (19) Defense counsel asked a non-expert witness about the

 5
 Case: 25-30381 Document: 58-1 Page: 6 Date Filed: 10/16/2026

 No. 25-30381

 “reasons why it’s important to tell the public to stick to agenda
 items only.” The Court directed defense counsel not to ask
 this question of a non-expert. Defense counsel continued, ask-
 ing next “why it’s important to keep people on time.”
 (20) Defense counsel stated, “everyone, except for you, seems
 to say that the only property, the only tracts of land that were
 in this new zoning application, the one that you wrote the ethics
 company about, was the property belonging to Greenfield,” to
 which the Court pointed out was “like testimony.”
 (21) Defense counsel stated, “First of all, Jaclyn Hotard is not
 the secretary of the parish counsel,” to which the Court inter-
 jected instructing defense counsel to stop testifying.
 (22) Defense counsel stated, “First and foremost, the Open
 Meetings Law requires that the agenda . . . .” The Court in-
 structed defense counsel to stop testifying.
 (23) Defense counsel stated, “You also saw that a couple other
 people—and if you don’t recall, I can show you a video of the
 meeting . . . .” The Court instructed defense counsel to ask a
 question and stop testifying.
 (24) Defense counsel attempted to provide Ms. Gaudet’s
 answer to a deposition question, to which the Court instructed
 defense counsel to ask a question and stop reading the
 deposition.
 (25) Defense counsel attempted to provide testimony about
 Ms. Gaudet’s deposition, to which the Court instructed, “You
 can’t refer to her deposition. You have to ask her a question
 because you’re not impeaching her.”
 (26) Defense counsel asked a witness, “The meetings, to be
 compliant with the Louisiana [O]pen [M]eetings [L]aw, must
 have some time period in which the public can discuss items
 that the council is going to vote on. Was that always done?”
 Plaintiff’s counsel objected, and the objection was overruled.
 (27) Defense counsel began to “testify” about what “we con-

 6

 No. 25-30381

 cluded” in Ms. Gulliot’s deposition. Plaintiff’s counsel ob-
 jected, and the objection was sustained.
 (28) Defense counsel talked about what letters were or were
 not stamped “confidential[,]” to which the Court advised that
 defense counsel was testifying again.
 (29) Defense counsel stated that Mr. Wright’s “testimony is
 [he] did not notice or read the particular note.” The Court
 instructed defense counsel that he cannot testify for the
 witness.
 (30) Defense counsel stated that “I saw you cleared the cham-
 ber on the video.” Plaintiff’s counsel objected, and the objec-
 tion was sustained.
 (31) Defense counsel stated that the facts were “falsely alleged
 by Ms. Banner.” Plaintiff’s counsel objected, and the objection
 was sustained. The jury was instructed to disregard the
 statement.
 (32) Defense counsel stated that Ms. Hotard’s reelection
 “seems like an incredible vote of confidence.” Plaintiff’s
 counsel objected, and the objection was sustained. The jury
 was instructed to disregard the statement.
 (33) During cross examination of Ms. Banner, defense counsel
 pulled out a timer and said, “I’m going to

SUPERIOR COURT OF NEW JERSEY 
 APPELLATE DIVISION 
 DOCKET NO . A-0591-25 

MARIA AGUIRRE, ANDREA 
PALACIOS and LORENA 
VARAS, 

 Plaintiffs -Respondents, 

v. 

CDL LAST MILE SOLUTIONS, 
LLC, SUBCONTRACTING 
CONCEPTS, LLC , d/b/a SCI, 
ANTHONY CURCIO, 

 Defendants -Appellants , 

and 

KATTY PONCE, 

 Defendant. 
_____________________________ 

Argued September 15, 2026 – Decided October 16, 2026 

Before Judges Rose and Natali. 

On appeal from the Superior Court of New Jersey, Law 
Division, Bergen County, Docket No. L -1172-23. 
NOT FOR PUBLICATION WITHOUT THE 
APPROVAL OF THE APPELLATE DIVISION 

This opinion shall not "constitute precedent or be binding upon any court ." Although it is posted on the 
internet , this opinion is binding only on the parties in the case and its use in other cases is limited . R. 1:36 -3. 

2 A-0591 -25 

Theodore Eder argued the cause for appellants CDL 
Last Mile Solutions, LLC and Anthony Curcio (Weber 
Gallagher, attorneys ; Theodore Eder, on the brief s). 

Scott Simpson (Menken Simpson & Rozger LLP) of the 
New York bar, admitted pro hac vice , argued the cause 
for respondents (A.Y. Strauss LLC , attorneys; Scott 
Simpson , Raya F. Saksouk, (Menken Simpson & 
Rozger LLP) of the New York bar, admitted pro hac 
vice, Daniel J. Cohen and Daniel C. Stark, of counsel 
and on the brief). 

PER CURIAM 

Defendants CDL Last Mile Solutions, LLC (CDL), Subcontracting 
Concepts, LLC d/b/a SCI (SCI) , and Anthony Curcio challenge two orders dated 
June 4, 2025 and September 25, 2025 . The June 4 o rder granted plaintiff s' 
application to certify this New Jersey Wage and Hour Law, N.J.S.A. 34:11-56a 
to -56a38 (NJWHL) , and New Jersey Wage Payment Law, N.J.S.A. 34:11 -4.1 
to -4.14 (NJWPL) , dispute as a class action, appointed class representatives and 
class counsel. On September 25 , the court modified its June 4 order by 
clarifying and expanding the class to include drivers based out of CDL 's 
Moonachie and Carlstadt facilities , while narrowing the class to exclude 
individuals classified by defendants as employees who oversaw work performed 
by delivery drivers. 

3 A-0591 -25 

Before us, defendants argue the court erred when it certified the class 
because plaintiffs ' counsel initially sued Katty Ponce, one of defendants ' former 
employees , whom they contend fell within the class as originally ple d which 
caused a permanent, disqualifying conflict . According to defendants, that 
conflict was not remedied by her later dismissal from the case or by the court 's 
exclusion of certain supervisory employees from the class pursuant to the 
September 25 order. Defendants also contend the: 1) record does not support 
the court 's finding that Ponce fell within th e terms of the September 25 order, 2) 
revised class definition improperly excluded individuals who otherwise 
belonged in the class, 3) class includes drivers who may be adverse to one 
another because some drivers allegedly hired or paid other drivers, and 4) 
certification was premature on an insufficiently developed record. 
After reviewing the record against the applicable legal principles, we are 
convinced the court properly exercised its discretion when it determined 
plaintiffs satisfied Rule 4:32-1, including subsection (a)(4)'s adequacy of 
representation prong, after the parties consented to the dismissal of Ponce with 
prejudice before certification and the class was later refined to exclude 
employees who oversaw work performed by delivery drivers. We further 
determine the court acted properly when it modified the class definition before 

4 A-0591 -25 

final judgment, and the record at the certification stage was sufficient to support 
that preliminary class-management decision. Finally, we are satisfied the court 
acted well within its discretion when it determined common questions 
concerning defendants ' classification and compensation practices predominated 
over any individualized issues, and when it concluded certification was 
appropriate without additional discovery. 
I. 
Defendant CDL is a regional delivery service specializing in logistics and 
last mile delivery services that operate s warehouses in Moonachie, Carlstadt, 
and Westampton . Defendant SCI, a Delaware LLC , headquartered in New York, 
"provides third -party administrative support for courier and logistics 
companies. " Defendant Curcio is the owner and operator of CDL. 
 Plaintiffs are New Jersey residents and work as delivery drivers for CDL . 
They make deliveries exclusively in New Jersey and report to either the 
Moonachie or Carlstadt warehouses . 
On March 2, 2023, plaintiffs filed a putative class action complaint 
seeking damages, injunctive and declaratory relief, attorneys ' fees and costs. 
The complaint allege d the class include d at least one hundred "delivery drivers 
who performed work for [d]efendants in the State of New Jersey from March 

5 A-0591 -25 

2017, until [d]efendants cease their unlawful acts. " Plaintiffs claimed they were 
misclassified as independent contractors and denied overtime pay in violation 
of the NJWHL. Plaintiffs also alleged defendants unlawfully deducted from 
their wages in violation of the NJWPL. 
Both CDL and SCI moved to dismiss the complaint under Rule 4:6-2(e), 
and to compel arbitration. The court denied their motions and stayed the 
litigation pending appeal . We affirmed , conclud ing New Jersey law applied, 
and that the arbitration agreements were unenforceable under Atalese v. U.S. 
Legal Servs. Grp., L.P. , 219 N.J. 430, 436 (2014) . See Aguirre v. CDL Last 
Mile Solutions, LLC , A-3346-22 (App. Div. Feb. 26, 2024) ( slip op. at 3 -4). 
The Supreme Court denied certification. Maria Aguirre, Andrea Palacios and 
Lorena Varas v. CDL, Anthony Curcio, Katty Ponce, and SCI , 257 N.J. 590 
(2024). 
On remand, plaintiffs moved to certify a class covering all delivery drivers 
based out of CDL 's "New Jersey warehouses " and for the appointment of class 
representatives and class counsel. Defendants opposed plaintiffs ' application 
and noted the complaint only alleged facts related to CDL's Moonachie facility. 
At oral argument, defendants raised a conflict of issue argument related 
to Ponce, a logistics coordinator who was also an owner/operator delivery driver 

6 A-0591 -25 

working out of the Moonachie warehouse. Defendants argued that plaintiffs ' 
initial decision to name Ponce as a defendant was a conflict of interest because 
she was a delivery driver who fell within the ir proposed class definition. They 
also asserted that Ponce was neither a manager nor a supervisor. 
When the court noted that Ponce appeared to be "managing on behalf of 
the company, " defendants ' counsel clarified she was only "hired to help 
coordinate in addition to her duties as a n . . . independent contractor. " Thus, 
defendants maintain ed she fit within the same general contractual and 
operational framework as other Moonachie drivers —namely, as one of CDL 's 
independent -contractor delivery operators contracting through SCI —and that 
any coordination responsibilities did not place her outside that group. Stated 
differently, defendants characterized Ponce as similar to the putative class 
members in both the nature of her delivery work and their respective contracts. 
Plaintiffs ' counsel disagreed with defendants ' characterization of Ponce 's 
role and maintained the proposed class of delivery drivers were "heavily 
supervised " by Ponce. Addressing the initial decision to name her as a 
defendant, plaintiffs contended they were unaware of the potential conflict issue 
and noted that defendants raised it approximately two years into the litigation. 
To address the se issues, the court requested supplemental briefing on the 

7 A-0591 -25 

potential conflict and other issues raised at oral argument . Shortly t hereafter, 
the parties agreed to stipulat e the dismissal of all claims as to Ponce with 
prejudice . 
On June 4, 2025, the court entered an order granting plaintiffs ' motion for 
class certification. Although the form order referred to delivery drivers based 
out of CDL's "New Jersey warehouse(s), " the court's accompanying written rider 
made clear the court was, at that time, limiting the certified class to drivers based 
out of the Moonachie warehouse. The court explained the record before it did 
not support certification with respect to drivers from the Carlstadt or 
Westampton facilities. 1 
In addition, in its June 4 rider, the court noted that plaintiffs had proposed 
excluding individuals who were, or had been, classified by defendants as 
employees who oversaw work performed by delivery drivers . The court did not 
formally incorporate that exclusion into the class definition until the September 
25 order. 

1 As discussed below at page ten, the discrepancy between the broader language 
in the order and the narrower limitation set forth in the rider was later addressed 
in the September 25 order, which expanded the class to include drivers based 
out of Moonachie and the Carlstadt predecessor facilities, but not Westampton, 
and also excluded individuals classified by defendants as employees who 
oversaw work performed by deli very drivers. 

8 A-0591 -25 

The court found that the Moonachie drivers were required to report on site 
every morning, perform several hours of work, and were under the direction and 
control of a Ponce, a New Jersey -based supervisor. The court specifically 
described Ponce as a "CDL dispatcher who was primarily responsible for 
supervising CDL 's New Jersey drivers. " Next, the court explained its reasons 
why plaintiffs satisfied Rule 4:32-1(a)(1) through (a)(4) . 
The court found plaintiffs ' proposed class included approximately one 
hundred and fifty individuals who w orked as delivery drivers. The court also 
determined there existed numerous common questions among plaintiffs and the 
putative class members. The court specifically found that plaintiffs satisfied 
Rule 4:32-1(a)(3)'s typicality requirement because plaintiffs sought to represent 
all CDL delivery drivers who were misclassified as independent contractors and 
therefore denied overtime pay for hours exceeding forty a week and allegedly 
suffered unlawful deductions from their wages . Further, the court determined 
plaintiffs ' interest aligned with the proposed class members and plaintiffs ' 
counsel were experienced litigators specializing in employment -related matters. 
Next, the court found plaintiffs satisfied Rule 4:31-(b)(3)'s predominance 
and superiority requirements , as each class member alleged they were 
misclassified as independent contractors and signed agreements drafted by SCI. 

9 A-0591 -25 

The court determined that this misclassification formed the basis of defendants ' 
failure to pay overtime to plaintiffs and the putative class members. The court 
also found a class action was a superior method of addressing the parties ' 
disputes rather than filing over one hundred separate actions. 
Defendants filed a motion for reconsideration with respect to the conflict 
of interest issue and, alternatively, to clarify the geographic scope of the class 
consistent with the June 4 rider. In support of their opposition , plaintiffs 
included the deposition of James Carr , a former facilities manager at the 
Moonachie and Carlstadt warehouses , in which he testified Ponce's job 
responsibilities included manager -related work. Carr added that he delegated to 
Ponce the responsibility of distributing driver numbers and login information. 
Ultimately, the court denied defendant 's motion for re consideration and 
found the initial decision to sue Ponce was not a violation of the Rules of 
Professional Conduct, specifically RPC 1.7 , that would preclude class 
certification. In addition, regardless of Ponce 's status, the court concluded she 
could pursue her claims in or outside the class.
