leads.text:
SUPERIOR COURT OF NEW JERSEY 
 APPELLATE DIVISION 
 DOCKET NO . A-2722-24 

PBNJ CAPITAL, LLC, 

 Plaintiff -Appellant, 

v. 

TOWNSHIP OF MONTVILLE 
and STACY KOSTKA, 
Municipal Clerk, 

 Defendants -Respondents. 
_____________________________ 

Argued September 16, 2026 – Decided October 16, 2026 

Before Judges Mayer, Vinci and Zazzali -Hogan. 

On appeal from the Superior Court of New Jersey, Law 
Division, Morris County, Docket No. L -1479-24. 

Juliana C. Canevascini argued the cause for appellant 
(Trenk Isabel Siddiqi & Shahdanian PC, attorneys; 
Richard D. Trenk and Juliana C. Canevascini, on the 
briefs). 

Dawn M. Sullivan argued the cause for respondents 
(Dorsey & Semrau , LLC, attorneys; Dawn M. Sullivan, 
of counsel and on the brief ; Fred C. Semrau, on the 
brief). 

NOT FOR PUBLICATION WITHOUT THE 
APPROVAL OF THE APPELLATE DIVISION 

This opinion shall not "constitute precedent or be binding upon any court." Although it is posted on the 
internet , this opinion is binding only on the parties in the case and its use in other cases is limited. R. 1:36 -3. 

2 A-2722 -24 

PER CURIAM 

 Plaintiff PBNJ Capital, LLC (PBNJ) appeals from an April 7, 2025 order 
denying its application for disclosure of documents by defendants Township of 
Montville (Township) and its municipal clerk, Stacy Kostka, under the Open 
Public Records Act (OPRA), N.J.S .A. 47:1A -1 to -13. For the reasons that 
follow, we vacate the April 7, 2025 order and remand for further proceedings . 
I. 
PBNJ is the owner of real property located at 16 Route 46 West in the 
Township, designated as Block 162, Lot 7 on the municipal tax map (PBNJ 
property). 12 Route 46 , LLC (12 Route 46), an affiliate of the Paul Miller Auto 
Group (PM Auto Group), is the owner of two adjacent properties, designated as 
Block 162, Lots 4 and 6 (12 Route 46 properties) (the PBNJ property and the 12 
Route 46 properties are referred to collectively as the properties). 
 On September 8, 2015, the Township Committee (Committee) adopted a 
resolution authorizing the Township Planning Board (Board) " to conduct a 
preliminary investigation to determine if an area, identified as the Westbound 
Route 46 Study Area," where the properties are located, "constituted an 'area in 
need of redevelopment ' as defined under the " Local Redevelopment and Housing 
Law (LRHL), N.J.S.A. 40A:12A -1 to -49. The Board retained Burgis 

3 A-2722 -24 

Associates, Inc. (Burgis) "to undertake an investigation and prepare a report." 
After reviewing Burgis's report, the Board "concluded . . . [the 
properties] . . . warranted inclusion in an Area in Need of Redevelopment 
[(Redevelopment Area)]." The Redevelopment Area was designated as a 
"condemnation area." 
On October 13, 2015, the Committee accepted the Board's findings and 
directed it to prepare a redevelopment plan. Burgis and the Board prepared a 
redevelopment plan, which the Committee adopted on September 27, 2016. 
In March 2020, the Township retained James Turteltaub, Esq. as special 
counsel related to the potential improvement of the Redevelopment Area. Along 
with Turteltaub, the Township was represented by Fred C. Semrau, Esq. and 
Dawn M. Sullivan, Esq. of Dorsey & Semrau. 12 Route 46 was represented by 
John Inglesino, Esq. and Allan Markus, Esq. of Inglesino, Webster, Wycis kala 
& Taylor, LLC. 
On June 24, 2020, 12 Route 46 "submitted a formal expression of 
development interest in becoming the 'designated redeveloper' of, and to 
redevelop, the entire Redevelopment Area." 12 Route 46 also submitted a 
"conceptual site plan and architectural plans" for the proposed redevelopment, 
which included "two . . . new car dealerships, one selling Honda automobiles 

4 A-2722 -24 

and one selling Toyota automobiles" (the Project). On September 22, 2020, the 
Committee adopted a resolution designating 12 Route 46 as the "[c]onditional 
[r]edeveloper of the Redevelopment Area" and authorizing the Township 
administrator to enter into a "[c]onditional [r]edevelopment [a]greement" with 
12 Route 46. 
That same day, the Township and 12 Route 46 entered into a " [s]hort 
[f]orm [r]edevelopment [a]greement" (Agreement) designating 12 Route 46 "as 
the exclusive [r]edeveloper of the" properties and granting 12 Route 46 "the 
exclusive right to pursue the Project" for a period of six months. The Agreement 
required 12 Route 46 to "contact [PBNJ] . . . and negotiate in good faith for the 
acquisition of the PBNJ [property] " for purposes of building the Project, and to 
"keep the Township apprised of such negotiations." 
According to Inglesino, the Township separately agreed that, because the 
Redevelopment Area was designated as a condemnation area, if 12 Route 46 was 
unable to negotiate the purchase of the P BNJ p roperty, "the Township was 
authorized . . . to exercise the power of eminent domain to acquire the [PBNJ] 
property in order to achieve the purposes of the designation." On April 27, 2021, 
the Committee adopted a resolution extending the term of the Agreem ent 
through August 22, 2021. 

5 A-2722 -24 

12 Route 46's efforts to purchase the PBNJ property were unsuccessful. 
On April 12, 2022, the Committee adopted a resolution directing the Board to 
"conduct an investigation to determine if the Westbound Route 46 Study 
Area . . . continued to qualify as an 'area in need of redevelopment. '" On June 
9, 2022, the Board adopted a resolution "conclud[ing] that a portion of the study 
area, to wit, [the properties ], continued to warrant inclusion in the [a]rea in 
[n]eed of [r]edevelopment." By way of a resolution dated June 10, 2022, the 
Committee "accepted the . . . Board's findings and report and re -designated [the 
properties] as an area in need of redevelopment." 
At or around this same time, because 12 Route 46's "efforts to acquire [the 
PBNJ property] for the construction of two [] dealerships ha[d] been 
unsuccessful," 12 Route 46 and the Township were engaged in "ongoing 
settlement negotiations." According to 12 Route 46, it "received notice" of the 
Committee's June 10 resolution on June 21 and had "until August 5, 2022, to 
file a legal action to challenge" the determination that the 12 Route 46 propert ies 
were "a condemnation area in need of redevelopment." On July 21, 2022, 12 
Route 46 and the Township agreed to "extend the subject statute of limitations 
period to September 30, 2022." The parties subsequently entered into additional 

6 A-2722 -24 

agreements, ultimately tolling 12 Route 46's time to file suit against the 
Township until January 13, 2023. 
On July 18, 2022, PBNJ filed a complaint in lieu of prerogative writs 
against the Township challenging its "blighting declaration, with condemnation 
rights" regarding the PBNJ property (PBNJ lawsuit). On September 27, 2022, 
the Committee passed a resoluti on removing the area's "condemnation" 
designation and directed Burgis to prepare a non -condemnation redevelopment 
plan. On October 25, 2022, the Committee passed a resolution adopting the non -
condemnation development plan prepared by Burgis. 
 On January 13, 2023, 12 Route 46 filed its own complaint in lieu of 
prerogative writs against the Township (12 Route 46 lawsuit). 12 Route 46 
claimed, among other things, that "[t]he determinations of both the [] Board and 
the [] Committee relative to the declaration of the [12 Route 46] [p]ropert [ies] 
as an area in need of redevelopment on a condemnation basis were arbitrary, 
capricious and unreasonable" and did "not satisfy any of the criteria set forth in 
N.J.S.A. 40A:12A -5." 
 On February 23, 2023, 12 Route 46 and the Township filed a stipulation 
dismissing the 12 Route 46 lawsuit without prejudice. On February 24, 2023, 
the court entered a consent order dismissing the PBNJ lawsuit without prejudice 

7 A-2722 -24 

in which the Township agreed, among other things, it would not "reimpose 
redevelopment with condemnation authority relative to [the PBNJ ] 
property . . . prior to January 24, 2026." 
II. 
On April 3, 2024, PBNJ submitted three OPRA requests to the Township, 
which were subsequently revised on April 11. The revised requests sought 
document s relating to communications concerning the PBNJ property sent or 
received by : (1) Township Administrator June Hercek ; (2) Semrau ; and (3) 
Sullivan. Specifically , they sought 
[a]ny and all text messages, e -mails, WhatsApp 
messages, records of phone calls and/or any messages 
sent through social media sites, sent or received by 
[Hercek , Semrau, or Sullivan] between June 13, 2016, 
and present concerning the [PBNJ] [p] roperty. This is 
to include any employee, representative or agent of the 
[PM] Auto Group including but not limited to: Allan 
Markus, Howard Hulin, Jim Ott, John Inglesino, and 
Christopher Ledoux. 

 In response, the Township produced Vaughn1 indexes listing 
communications it contended were exempt from disclosure under OPRA. The 
first, relating to Sullivan's communications (the Sullivan index), identifie d 
several "[e]mail chains" the Towns hip contended were exempt from disclosure 

1 Vaughn v. Rosen , 484 F.2d 820 (D.C. Cir. 1973) . 

8 A-2722 -24 

as advisory, consultative, and deliberative pursuant to N.J.S.A. 47:1A -1.1 (ACD 
exemption ). The second, relating to Semrau's communications (the Semrau 
index), identified several text messages, letters, and "[e]mail chains" the 
Township contended were exempt from disclosure pursuant to the ACD 
exemption. Both the Sullivan and Semrau index es also noted: "[v]arious emails 
between [] Semrau and [] Township representatives and co -counsel subject to 
attorney -client privilege." 
The third index related to Hercek's communications . It identified one 
"[e]mail chain" and one "[e]mail attachment" the Township contended were 
exempt from disclosure pursuant to both the attorney -client privilege and the 
ACD exemption , and a nother "[e]mail chain" the Township contended was 
exempt from disclosure pursuant only to the ACD exemption. 
 On July 31, 2024, PBNJ file d a verified complaint and order to show cause 
(OTSC) seeking the disclosure of the documents under OPRA by way of a 
summary action pursuant to Rule 4:67-1(a).2 On August 6, the court entered the 
OTSC. On November 1, after defendants filed their response to the OTSC, the 
court conducted an initial hearing , during which it, sua sponte, question ed 

2 OPRA provides that actions challenging a decision to withhold access to 
government records shall proceed in a "summary or expedited manner." 
N.J.S.A. 47:1A -6. 

9 A-2722 -24 

whether PBNJ's complaint was timely filed and ordered briefing on that issue . 
The parties also argued the merits of the Township's claims regarding the 
documents identified to that point. 
 On December 23, 2024 , the court entered an order, supported by a written 
statement of reasons, finding PBNJ's complaint was filed within the applicable 
forty-five-day statute of limitations . The court also ordered defendants to 
"submit a Vaughn index . . . for the records [they] claim [ed] [were] protected by 
attorney -client privilege" and "produce for in camera review documents they 
claim[ed] [were] pre-decisional and deliberative." 
 By letter dated January 13, 2025, defendants delivered to the court a 
"combined [a]ttorney/[c]lient [p]rivil eged [c]ommunications [l]og [(ACP log)] " 
and "Bates[ -s]tamped" copies of the documents identified in the Hercek, 
Sullivan, and Semrau indexes. Defendants did not send PBNJ a copy of the 
January 13 transmittal letter , nor did they provide a copy of the ACP log to 
PBNJ. On January 17, counsel for PBNJ wrote to Sullivan asking if defendants 
complied with the court's December 23, 2024 order. On January 20, Sullivan 
responded, that "[t]he court was provided with the Bates[ -s]tamped documents 
utilizing the [ Vaughn] [i]ndexes filed with [PBNJ's OTSC]. " Sullivan did not 
advise PBNJ that defendants also provided the ACP log to the co

leads.caseName: Commercial Properties, Inc. v. Ourania Charalambidou, Dionysios Mitsios, and Montgomery Civic Ballet, Inc., d/b/a Montgomery Ballet Studios
leads.text:
Rel: October 16, 2026

Notice: This opinion is subject to formal revision before publication in the advance sheets of Southern
Reporter. Readers are requested to notify the Reporter of Decisions, Alabama Appellate Courts,
300 Dexter Avenue, Montgomery, Alabama 36104-3741 ((334) 229-0650), of any typographical or other
errors, in order that corrections may be made before the opinion is printed in Southern Reporter.

 SUPREME COURT OF ALABAMA
 OCTOBER TERM, 2026-2027

 _________________________

 SC-2026-0190
 _________________________

 Commercial Properties, Inc.

 v.

 Ourania Charalambidou, Dionysios Mitsios, and Montgomery
 Civic Ballet, Inc., d/b/a Montgomery Ballet Studios

 _________________________

 SC-2026-0191
 _________________________

 Ourania Charalambidou, Dionysios Mitsios, and Montgomery
 Civic Ballet, Inc., d/b/a Montgomery Ballet Studios
 SC-2026-0190 and SC-2026-0191

 v.

 Commercial Properties, Inc.

 Appeals from Montgomery Circuit Court
 (CV-21-900117)

SELLERS, Justice.

 These consolidated appeals involve two commercial leases executed

by Commercial Properties, Inc. ("the landlord"), and Montgomery Civic

Ballet, Inc., doing business as Montgomery Ballet Studios ("the Ballet").

Dionysios Mitsios ("Danny") is the executive director of the Ballet, and

Ourania Charalambidou ("Rania") is his wife. In appeal no. SC-2026-

0191, the Ballet, Danny, and Rania appeal from separate orders of the

Montgomery Circuit Court ("the trial court"), striking as untimely their

response to the landlord's motion for a partial summary judgment and

subsequently denying the resubmission of that response. We affirm. In

appeal no. SC-2026-0190, the landlord cross-appeals from the trial court's

February 3, 2026, order certifying its motion for a partial summary

judgment as final pursuant to Rule 54(b), Ala. R. Civ. P., while, at the

 2
 SC-2026-0190 and SC-2026-0191

same time, purportedly dismissing the entire case. We affirm in part,

reverse in part, and remand.

 I. Facts

 The landlord and the Ballet entered into two separate lease

agreements in May 2008 and January 2012, respectively, pursuant to

which the landlord leased to the Ballet two suites located in a shopping

center owned and managed by the landlord. The lease agreements

contained a provision for indemnification by the tenant, a default

provision, and a provision outlining when the tenant would be liable for

attorney fees and costs incurred by the landlord.1 In December 2020, the

Ballet vacated the premises based on the landlord's alleged failure to

eliminate mold that existed in the leased premises.

 In January 2021, the Ballet, Danny, and Rania filed a multicount

complaint against the landlord, alleging that Danny and Rania had

suffered personal injuries after being exposed to mold in the leased

premises. The Ballet also claimed that the mold had caused damage to

its personal property, including its costumes. The landlord answered the

 1The Ballet, Danny, and Rania do not challenge the provisions of

the lease agreements upon which the landlord relied in seeking a partial
summary judgment; therefore, we do not quote or discuss them.
 3
 SC-2026-0190 and SC-2026-0191

complaint and filed a counterclaim, seeking unpaid rent under the lease

agreements and defense and indemnity from the Ballet on the claims

asserted by Danny and Rania. The landlord thereafter sent the Ballet a

letter demanding that the Ballet defend and indemnify it on the claims

asserted by Danny and Rania, as required by the lease agreements. The

Ballet did not respond to that demand.

 In February 2023, the landlord filed a motion for a partial summary

judgment, supported by various documents. The motion for a partial

summary judgment addressed only the claims involving the Ballet, and

not Danny's and Rania's claims against the landlord. In that motion, the

landlord sought

 "(1) an interlocutory judgment declaring that [the Ballet]
 owes [the landlord] $65,827.50 in unpaid rent, the judgment
 to become a final judgment after the amount of prejudgment
 interest and fees are submitted to [the trial court]; (2) [an]
 interlocutory judgment declaring that [the] Ballet owes [the
 landlord] defense and indemnity on the claims asserted
 against it by [Danny and Rania], the claims to become a final
 judgment at the time all claims in this matter are adjudicated
 and the total amount of attorneys' fees are submitted; and (3)
 [a] final judgment against the Ballet and in favor of [the
 landlord] on [the] Ballet's claims against it. There are no
 issues as to any material fact, and [the landlord] is entitled to
 [a] judgment as a matter of law on these claims."

 4
 SC-2026-0190 and SC-2026-0191

 On March 25, 2025, the trial court entered an order setting a

hearing on the partial-summary-judgment motion for April 21, 2025, at

10:00 a.m.2 On April 18, 2025, the Ballet, Danny, and Rania filed their

response in opposition to the partial-summary-judgment motion. Before

the hearing commenced, the landlord filed a motion to strike the response

as untimely. Following the hearing, the trial court entered an order

granting the motion to strike, thus leaving the motion for a partial

summary judgment unopposed. However, the trial court did not enter an

order on the partial-summary-judgment motion -- presumably because of

an oversight.

 On October 20, 2025, the landlord moved the trial court to enter an

order on its motion for a partial summary judgment. The trial court

entered an order setting the matter for a hearing on December 3, 2025,

noting that all "pending motions" would be heard at that time. The

 2According to the landlord, the delay between the filing of the
motion for a partial summary judgment in February 2023 and the
scheduling of the hearing in March 2025 was not caused by any action or
inaction on behalf of the parties. Rather, the landlord points out that
Judge Johnny Hardwick, the original circuit-court judge assigned to hear
the matter, was assaulted while the action was pending and suffered
severe injuries that kept him from his duties. Shortly after setting the
April 21, 2025, hearing, Judge Hardwick retired, and the case was
assigned to Circuit Court Judge Tiffany McCord.
 5
 SC-2026-0190 and SC-2026-0191

Ballet, Danny, and Rania filed a "response" to the landlord's motion for

an order on the partial summary judgment, and they resubmitted the

same response that the trial court had previously deemed untimely. The

landlord filed a motion to strike the response, arguing that the trial court

had already entered an order striking it as untimely.

 On December 22, 2025, following a hearing, the trial court entered

an order denying the "renewed" response filed by the Ballet, Danny, and

Rania and entering a partial summary judgment in favor of the landlord.

The Ballet, Danny, and Rania moved the trial court to certify the partial

summary judgment in favor of the landlord as final pursuant to Rule

54(b), Ala. R. Civ. P.

 On February 3, 2026, the trial court entered an order certifying the

partial summary judgment in favor of the landlord as final pursuant to

Rule 54(b) and indicating that "this case is dismissed." This appeal and

cross-appeal followed.

 II. Standard of Review

 "This Court's review of a summary judgment is de novo.
 Williams v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 886 So. 2d 72, 74
 (Ala. 2003). We apply the same standard of review as the trial
 court applied. Specifically, we must determine whether the
 movant has made a prima facie showing that no genuine issue
 of material fact exists and that the movant is entitled to a
 6
 SC-2026-0190 and SC-2026-0191

 judgment as a matter of law. Rule 56(c), Ala. R. Civ. P.; Blue
 Cross & Blue Shield of Alabama v. Hodurski, 899 So. 2d 949,
 952-53 (Ala. 2004)."

Dow v. Alabama Democratic Party, 897 So. 2d 1035, 1038 (Ala. 2004). A

trial court's decision to strike an untimely submission offered in response

to a motion for a summary judgment is reviewed under an excess-of-

discretion standard of review. Speer v. Pin Palace Bowling Alley, 599 So.

2d 1140 (Ala. 1992).

 III. Discussion

 A. Appeal No. SC-2026-0191 -- Timeliness of Opposition

 In their appeal, the Ballet, Danny, and Rania ("the plaintiffs") do

not challenge the merits of the partial summary judgment entered in

favor of the landlord.3 Rather, they challenge only the April 21, 2025,

order striking as untimely their response to the partial summary-

judgment motion and the December 22, 2025, order denying that same

response. The plaintiffs first claim that their response was timely

 3For the first time in their reply brief, the plaintiffs attempted to

challenge the merits of the partial summary judgment. However, we will
not consider their arguments. See Lloyd Noland Hosp. v. Durham, 906
So. 2d 157, 173 (Ala. 2005) ("It is a well-established principle of appellate
review that we will not consider an issue not raised in an appellant's
initial brief, but raised only in the reply brief.").
 7
 SC-2026-0190 and SC-2026-0191

because, they say, it was filed three calendar days before the April 21,

2025, hearing. However, the plaintiffs fail to acknowledge the interplay

between Rule 56(c)(2), Ala. R. Civ. P., and Rule 6(a), Ala. R. Civ. P.,

concerning the computation of periods specified in the rules. Rule

56(c)(2) provides that a "motion for summary judgment, with all

supporting materials, including any briefs, shall be served at least ten

(10) days before the time fixed for the hearing" and that responses in

opposition to a summary-judgment motion must be served two days

before the hearing on the motion. The version of Rule 6(a) in effect at the

time the partial-summary-judgment motion was filed provided that, in

computing any period specified in the rules, "the day of the act, event, or

default from which the designated period of time begins to run shall not

be included" and that, when a filing must be accomplished within 11 days

or less, "intermediate Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays shall be

excluded in the computation." Therefore, pursuant to Rule 56(c) and Rule

6(a), the day of the hearing on the partial-summary-judgment motion

(April 21) and the Saturday and Sunday preceding the hearing (April 19

and 20) are excluded from computation; thus, any response in opposition

was due on Thursday, April 17, 2025, two business days before the

 8
 SC-2026-0190 and SC-2026-0191

hearing. See Elliott Builders, Inc. v. Timbercreek Prop. Owners Ass'n,

128 So. 3d 755, 765 (Ala. Civ. App. 2013) (indicating that Rule 56(c)(2)

"requires that matters in opposition to a summary-judgment motion

must be filed and served two days (i.e., two business days, see Rule 6(a),

Ala. R. Civ. P.) before the hearing on the motion"). Accordingly, the filing

of the response on the Friday before the scheduled hearing on Monday

was untimely.

 The plaintiffs also contend that, by striking their response in

opposition to the landlord's partial-summary-judgment motion, they

were denied the opportunity to be heard on both the partial-summary-

judgment motion and the motion to strike their response. The plaintiffs

cite Moore v. Prudential Residential Services Ltd. Partnership, 849 So.

2d 914, 926 (Ala. 2002) ("Rule 56(c)(2), Ala. R. Civ. P., gives the

nonmoving party certain rights to notice and a hearing after a summary-

judgment motion has been filed."). However, it is clear that the plaintiffs

had notice of both the April 21, 2025, hearing on the motion for a partial

summary judgment and the motion to strike that was filed and ruled

upon on that same date. To the extent that counsel for the plaintiffs failed

 9
 SC-2026-0190 and SC-2026-0191

to attend that hearing, we will not fault the trial court for that absence.4

Furthermore, although the plaintiffs assert that the requirements of

Rule 56(c)(2) are procedural in nature and that a trial court is afforded

errors, in order that corrections may be made before the opinion is printed in Southern Reporter.

 SUPREME COURT OF ALABAMA
 OCTOBER TERM, 2026-2027

 _________________________

 SC-2025-0803
 _________________________

 Ex parte City of Fairhope Planning Commission and City of
 Fairhope

 PETITION FOR WRIT OF MANDAMUS

 (In re: 68V BTR Holdings, LLC

 v.

 City of Fairhope Planning Commission and City of Fairhope)

 (Baldwin Circuit Court: CV-24-900981)

PARKER, Justice.
 SC-2025-0803

 68V BTR Holdings, LLC, wanted to develop two pieces of property

in the City of Fairhope, but Fairhope's Planning Commission denied

68V's project applications. 68V has challenged those denials on various

grounds, some of which are currently pending in the circuit court. For

now, though, only one of those grounds matters -- a claim for money

damages against the City and the Planning Commission premised on the

alleged negligence of the Planning Commission and City employees in

denying the applications.

 Below, the City and the Planning Commission sought summary

judgment on this claim based on a combination of three different species

of immunity. But the circuit court denied that request. The City and the

Planning Commission now petition this Court for a writ of mandamus

directing the circuit court to enter judgment for the City and the Planning

Commission on 68V's negligence claim. Because both the City and the

Planning Commission are immune with respect to the negligence claim,

we grant the petition and issue the writ.

 I.

 The City created the Planning Commission and tasked it with

making decisions concerning the approval of subdivisions in accordance

 2
 SC-2025-0803

with the City's subdivision regulations. Cf. Ala. Code 1975, § 11-52-1 et

seq. The Commission consists of nine members who serve on a volunteer

basis. To assist the planning commissioners in fulfilling their duties, the

City employs planning staff; the Commission has no staff of its own.

 68V filed applications with the Planning Commission seeking to

develop two townhome apartment complexes, one named "Skyline

Village" and the other named "Gables on Lawrence." Ultimately, the

Planning Commission denied those applications. According to meeting

minutes, the Planning Commission denied the Gables application

because of "adverse drainage effects," because certain "greenspace"

requirements were not met, because it failed to meet the Planning

Commission's "Comprehensive Plan," and because of "traffic problems."

According to the Commission meeting's minutes, it denied the Skyline

application because of "drainage issues" as well as issues concerning

"traffic," "health, safety and general welfare."

 Dissatisfied by the denials, 68V sued the City and the Planning

Commission. 68V did not initially seek mandamus review in state court

to compel compliance with the relevant statutes. Cf. T Invs., LLC v. City

of Montgomery Plan. Comm'n, 393 So. 3d 55, 63 (Ala. 2023). Instead, 68V

 3
 SC-2025-0803

initially sued the City and the Planning Commission in federal district

court. After the federal court resolved all the federal claims against 68V

and declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over 68V's state-law

claims, 68V then refiled in state court. There, it sought damages against

the City and the Planning Commission based on their (or their

employees') alleged negligence "in the consideration and/or denial of [the]

applications." 68V's operative state-court complaint also asserted two

other claims -- one for equitable relief invalidating the denials based on

an alleged "arbitrary and capricious" denial of 68V's applications and

another for damages based on an alleged deprivation of 68V's property

"without substantive due process of law" under the Alabama

Constitution.

 The City and the Planning Commission answered the amended

complaint and moved for summary judgment on all three of 68V's claims.

With respect to the negligence claim, the City and the Planning

Commission argued that the claim was barred by municipal immunity,

see § 11-47-190, Ala. Code 1975; volunteer immunity, see § 6-5-336(d),

Ala. Code 1975; and substantive immunity. The circuit court denied the

 4
 SC-2025-0803

summary-judgment motion, and this petition followed. This petition

seeks mandamus relief regarding only 68V's claim of negligence.

 II.

 As always, this Court will grant mandamus relief only when the

petitioner shows (1) a clear legal right to the order sought; (2) the trial

court's refusal to perform some "imperative duty"; (3) the lack of another

adequate remedy (such as an appeal); and (4) that it has properly invoked

the Court's jurisdiction. Ex parte Runnels, 364 So. 3d 979, 982 (Ala. 2022)

(citation modified).

 Most of these prerequisites are not in dispute here. The circuit court

issued a written order denying the City and the Planning Commission's

immunity-based request for summary judgment, and this Court has held

that there is no viable alternative remedy for the wrongful denial of such

a request. See Ex parte Butts, 775 So. 2d 173, 176 (Ala. 2000). We also

perceive no jurisdictional problem in reviewing the City and the Planning

Commission's petition. For these reasons, the dispositive question boils

down to whether the City and the Planning Commission have shown a

clear legal right to such an order.

 5
 SC-2025-0803

 III.

 The City and the Planning Commission have carried this burden.

68V's claims against the City and the Planning Commission rely on a

theory of respondeat superior -- the notion that the City and the Planning

Commission should be held responsible for the on-the-job acts and

omissions of their agents. The converse of this principle is also true: If

the City and Planning Commission's agents are not liable, because of

immunity or otherwise, then the City and the Planning Commission also

cannot be liable based on those agents' actions. See Murey v. City of

Chickasaw, 385 So. 3d 903, 917-18 (Ala. 2023); Hollis v. City of Brighton,

885 So. 2d 135, 141-42 (Ala. 2004). Here, 68V has asserted that the City

and the Planning Commission should be held responsible for the

negligence of two categories of agents: the members of the Planning

Commission, on one hand, and certain city employees, on the other. For

the reasons that follow, both categories of agents are immune from 68V's

negligence claim. The City and the Planning Commission are thus also

immune.

 6
 SC-2025-0803

 A.

 The members of the Planning Commission are entitled to

"volunteer immunity" under Alabama's Volunteer Service Act, Ala. Code

1975, § 6-5-336. 68V alleged that these commissioners acted "negligently,

neglectfully, carelessly or unskillfully" in considering or denying 68V's

applications. But as the City and the Planning Commission point out,

the Volunteer Service Act provides immunity for municipal volunteers if

they (1) were acting in "good faith" within the scope of their official

"functions and duties" and (2) were not engaged in "willful or wanton

misconduct." § 6-5-336(d). Under Alabama law, "[a]ll members of [a city

planning] commission shall serve without compensation," Ala. Code

1975, § 11-52-3(b), so the commissioners unquestionably qualify as

volunteers for a "governmental entity," § 6-5-336(d). Their consideration

and denial of 68V's applications is likewise "within the scope of [their]

official functions and duties." Id.; see Ala. Code 1975, § 11-52-32(a)

(authorizing municipal planning commissions to "approve or disapprove"

proposed plats). And 68V does not claim that the commissioners were

acting willfully or wantonly. As a result, the planning commissioners are

 7
 SC-2025-0803

immune from any alleged negligence in declining to approve 68V's

applications.

 68V attempts to bring the planning commissioners' actions outside

the scope of volunteer immunity by asserting that the commissioners

acted in bad faith. But Alabama's municipal-immunity statute "limits a

municipality's liability for the acts of its agents to those acts that are

negligent, careless, or unskillful." Ex parte City of Tuskegee, 932 So. 2d

895, 910 (Ala. 2005) (applying Ala. Code 1975, § 11-47-190). The upshot,

as this Court has explained, is that the municipal-immunity statute also

immunizes "the acts of [municipal] agents that are carried out in bad

faith …." Id.1

 1There does not appear to be any dispute between the parties that

the Planning Commission is entitled to municipal immunity in the same
way that the City is. Indeed, because the Planning Commission was
created by the City and acted as an administrative body of the City, it is
entitled to the protections of municipal immunity. See Hilliard v. City of
Huntsville Elec. Util. Bd., 599 So. 2d 1108, 1110 n.2 (Ala. 1992)
(recognizing that an entity is entitled to municipal immunity if it is
created by a city to serve as " 'a department or administrative arm ' " of
that city (quoting C. Keating and J. Perkowitz-Solheim, McQuillin's Law
of Municipal Corporations § 53.05b (3d ed., 1984 & 1991 Cum. Supp.));
and Mobile City Plan. Comm'n v. Stanely, 775 So. 2d 226, 228 (Ala. Civ.
App. 2000) ("When a planning commission exercises control over
subdivision lands within a municipality it acts in an administrative
capacity.").

 8
 SC-2025-0803

 68V argues that conduct can be in bad faith while still counting as

negligence, thus sliding between the volunteer-immunity statute and the

municipal-immunity statute. This argument, however, is squarely

foreclosed by our cases holding that the municipal-immunity statute

precludes claims arising out of alleged bad-faith conduct. See, e.g., Rogers

v. Cedar Bluff Volunteer Fire Dep't, [Ms. SC-2025-0055, Aug. 29, 2025]

__ So. 3d __, ___ n.10 (Ala. 2025); see also Ex parte City of Tuskegee, 932

So. 2d at 910. If the planning commissioners acted negligently, then

volunteer immunity prevents this suit. If the planning commissioners

acted in bad faith, then municipal immunity prevents this suit. Either

way, 68V's suit against the City and the Planning Commission for

negligence cannot proceed based on the actions or inactions of the

planning commissioners.

 B.

 68V also contends that the City and the Planning Commission are

liable for negligence by certain nonvolunteer City employees. Although

these paid City employees are ineligible for volunteer immunity under

the Volunteer Service Act, they are immune for a different reason: the

doctrine of substantive immunity. This doctrine does not foreclose

 9
 SC-2025-0803

traditional means of compelling governmental compliance with state law,

such as a writ of mandamus. Cf. T Invs., 393 So. 3d at 63. But it does

provide immunity from tort liability for those governmental activities "so

laden with the public interest as to outweigh the incidental duty to

individual citizens." See Ex parte City of Muscle Shoals, 384 So. 3d 37,

41 (Ala. 2023) (citation modified). The idea is that, when government

actors are discharging some generalized duty owed to the public at large,

accountability should come at the ballot box rather than from judges

usurping the roles of elected local officials.

 Here, 68V argues that three city employees were all negligent for

various roles they played in providing staff support to the Planning

Commission:

  The City Planning Director. According to 68V, the City's
 Planning Director relied on improper factors such as the City's
 "greenspace" requirements and the Planning Commission's
 comprehensive plan to recommend denial of the Gables
 application. 68V also argues that the City Pla

leads.caseName: In re: Angel Morales Cuin, as personal representative of the Estate of Ricardo Morales Cuin v. The City of Birmingham and Alonzo Cornelious Coleman IV
leads.text:
Rel: October 16, 2026 

Notice: This opinion is subject to formal revision before publication in the advance sheets of Southern 
Reporter. Readers are requested to notify the Reporter of Decisions, Alabama Appellate Courts, 
300 Dexter Avenue, Montgomery, Alabama 36104-3741 ((334) 229-0650), of any typographical or other 
errors, in order that corrections may be made before the opinion is printed in Southern Reporter. 

SUPREME COURT OF ALABAMA 

OCTOBER TERM, 2026-2027 
_________________________ 

SC-2025-0482 
_________________________ 

Ex parte Alonzo Cornelius Coleman IV and The City of 
Birmingham 

PETITION FOR WRIT OF MANDAMUS 

(In re: Angel Morales Cuin, as personal representative of the 
Estate of Ricardo Morales Cuin, deceased 

v. 

The City of Birmingham and Alonzo Cornelius Coleman IV) 

(Jefferson Circuit Court: CV-22-901939) 

SC-2025-0482 
2 

BRYAN, Justice.1 

 Alonzo Cornelius Coleman IV, a police officer employed by the 
Birmingham Police Department ("the police department"), and the City 
of Birmingham ("the city ") petition this Court for a writ of mandamus 
directing the Jefferson Circuit Cour t to enter a summary judgment in 
their favor on the ground that they are entitled to immunity. We grant 
the petition and issue the writ. 
Factual Background and Procedural History 
 Officer Coleman was on patrol on the night of Ja nuary 15, 2022, 
when the police car that he was dr iving struck Ricardo Morales Cuin 
("Ricardo") as he was walking on Tarrant-Huffman Road in Birmingham. 
Ricardo died as a result of the collis ion. The accident occurred slightly 
after 11:00 p.m. during a rainfall. At the time of the accident, Officer 
Coleman was listening to a podcast pl aying on his personal cell phone; 
the cell phone was resting on his bag on the passenger seat. In his 
deposition, Officer Coleman testifie d that he had recently begun his 
patrol and that he had started playin g the podcast when he had been at 

1This case was previously assigned to another justice on this Court 
before it was reassigned to Justice Bryan on June 15, 2026. 
SC-2025-0482 
3 

the police station earlier. He testified that he did not see Ricardo before 
the collision. The speed limit on Ta rrant-Huffman Road at the location 
of the accident was 35 miles per hour ; as we will discuss below, there is 
conflicting evidence regarding whether Officer Coleman was speeding at 
the time. Ricardo was wearing dark clothing, and the coroner's report 
indicates that he was intoxicated. 
Ricardo's brother, Ange l Morales Cuin ("Angel"), as the personal 
representative of Ricardo's estate, sued Officer Coleman and the city, 
alleging a claim of wrongful death ag ainst each defendant. Angel sued 
Officer Coleman in both his official and individual capacities. The 
wrongful-death claim against Office r Coleman was based on theories of 
negligence and wantonness, and the wrongful-death claim against the 
city was based on the th eory of vicarious liability. Officer Coleman and 
the city each moved for a summary judgment, asserting various grounds. 
In relevant part, Officer Coleman and the city asserted that the official-
capacity claim against Officer Coleman is barred by State immunity and 
that the individual-capacity claim against him is barred by State-agent 
immunity. The city further asserted that it is not vicariously liable for 
Ricardo's death because, the city sa id, Officer Coleman is immune. The 
SC-2025-0482 
4 

circuit court entered a partial summ ary judgment in favor of Officer 
Coleman on the wrongful-death claim filed against him in his official 
capacity, concluding that that clai m is barred by State immunity. The 
circuit court denied the summary-jud gment motion as to the wrongful-
death claim filed against Officer Coleman in his individual capacity and 
as to the wrongful-death claim agains t the city. In relevant part, the 
circuit court concluded that Officer Coleman is not entitled to State-agent 
immunity regarding the individual-capacity claim. Officer Coleman and 
the city then filed a mandamus petiti on with this Cour t, arguing that 
Officer Coleman is entitled to State-agent immunity and that the circuit 
court erred by not entering a summary judgment on all claims. 
Standard of Review 
The general rule is that the denial of a summary-judgment motion 
is not reviewable. However, an exception to that general rule exists here: 
the denial of a summary-judgment motion grounded on a claim of 
immunity is reviewable by a mandam us petition. Ex parte Turner, 840 
So. 2d 132, 135 (Ala. 2002). 
" A writ of mandamus is an extraordinary remedy, and 
it will be 'issued only when th ere is: 1) a clear legal right in 
the petitioner to the order sought; 2) an imperative duty upon 
the respondent to perform, accompanied by a refusal to do so; 
SC-2025-0482 
5 

3) the lack of another adequate remedy; and 4) properly 
invoked jurisdiction of the co urt.' Ex parte United Serv. 
Stations, Inc., 628 So. 2d 501, 503 (Ala. 1993)." 

Ex parte Empire Fire & Marine Ins. Co., 720 So. 2d 893, 894 (Ala. 1998). 

"In reviewing a trial court' s ruling on a motion for a 
summary judgment, we apply th e same standard the trial 
court applied initially in granting or denying the motion. Ex 
parte Alfa Mut. Gen. Ins. Co., 742 So. 2d 182, 184 (Ala. 1999). 

" 'The principles of law applicable to a motion 
for summary judgment are well settled. To grant 
such a motion, the trial court must determine that 
the evidence does not create a genuine issue of 
material fact and that the movant is entitled to 
judgment as a matter of law. Rule 56(c)(3), Ala. R. 
Civ. P. When the movant makes a prima facie 
showing that those two co nditions are satisfied, 
the burden shifts to th e nonmovant to present 
"substantial evidence" creating a genuine issue of 
material fact.' 

"742 So. 2d at 184. '[S]ubstantial evidence is evidence of such 
weight and quality that fair-minded persons in the exercise of 
impartial judgment can reasonabl y infer the existence of the 
fact sought to be proved.' We st v. Founders Life Assurance 
Co. of Florida, 547 So. 2d 870, 871 (Ala. 1989)." 

Swan v. City of Hueytown, 920 So . 2d 1075, 1077-78 (Ala. 2005). " 'Our 
review [of the circuit court's ruling on a summary-judgment motion] is 
further subject to the caveat that this Court must review the record in a 
light most favorable to the nonmov ant and must resolve all reasonable 
doubts against the movant.' " Harper v. Coats, 988 So. 2d 501, 503 (Ala. 
SC-2025-0482 
6 

2008) (quoting Hobson v. American Ca st Iron Pipe Co., 690 So. 2d 341, 
344 (Ala. 1997)). 
Discussion 
I. 
Officer Coleman and the city argue that Officer Coleman is entitled 
to State-agent immunity as defined by Ex parte Cranman, 792 So. 2d 392 
(Ala. 2000), and § 6-5-338(a), Ala. Code 1975.2 
"[P]eace officers are afforded immunity by Ala. Code 1975, § 
6-5-338(a), and the test for State-agent immunity set forth in 
Ex parte Cranman, 792 So. 2d 392 (Ala. 2000), as modified in 
Hollis v. City of Brighton, 950 So. 2d 300 (Ala. 2006) 
(incorporating the pe ace-officer-immunity standard provided 
in § 6-5-338(a) into the State-ag ent-immunity analysis found 
in Cranman). See Ex parte Ke nnedy, 992 So. 2d 1276 (Ala. 
2008), and City of Birmingham v. Brown, 969 So. 2d 910, 916 
(Ala. 2007) ('Immunity applies to employees of municipalities 
in the same manner that immu nity applies to employees of 
the State.' (citing Cranman, supra))." 

2Cranman was a plurality decision, but a majority of this Court 
later adopted the Cranman standard in Ex parte Butts, 775 So. 2d 173 
(Ala. 2000). In 2025, the Legislature repealed § 6-5-338 and replaced it 
with § 6-5-338.1 et seq., Ala. Code 1975. The new law applies "to any 
cause of action that accrued on or after October 1, 2025." § 6-5-338.4(a), 
Ala. Code 1975. Because this action accrued before that date, the new 
law does not apply here. 
SC-2025-0482 
7 

Suttles v. Roy, 75 So. 3d 90, 94 (Ala . 2010). In relevant part, Cranman, 
as modified by this Court in Hollis v. City of Brighton, 950 So. 2d 300 
(Ala. 2006), provides: 
"[A] State agent shall be immu ne from civil liability in 
his or her personal capacity when the conduct made the basis 
of the claim against the agent is based upon the agent's 

"…. 

"(4) exercising judgment in the enforcement of the 
criminal laws of the State, in cluding, but not limited to, law-
enforcement officers' arresting or attempting to arrest 
persons[, or serving as peace officers under circumstances 
entitling such officers to immu nity pursuant to § 6-5-338(a), 
Ala. Code 1975]." 

792 So. 2d at 405 (the bracketed lang uage is the modification added by 
Hollis, see 950 So. 2d at 309). 
However, there are two exceptions to State-agent immunity. Even 
if a State agent's conduct falls with in a Cranman category of immunity 
(such as the fourth category quoted above), a State agent will not be 
entitled to immunity 
"(1) when the Constitution or laws of the United States, 
or the Constitution of this State, or laws, rules, or regulations 
of this State enacted or pr omulgated for the purpose of 
regulating the activities of a governmental agency require 
otherwise; or 

SC-2025-0482 
8 

"(2) when the State agent ac ts willfully, maliciously, 
fraudulently, in bad faith, beyo nd his or her authority, or 
under a mistaken interpretation of the law." 

Cranman, 792 So. 2d at 405 (emphasis added). 

A defendant asserting State-agent immunity has the initial burden 
of establishing that his or her rele vant conduct falls under one of the 
enumerated categories of State- agent immunity established by 
Cranman. Ex parte Kennedy, 992 So . 2d 1276, 1282 (Ala. 2008). If the 
defendant establishes that the rele vant conduct falls under a Cranman 
category, the burden then shifts to th e plaintiff to show that one of the 
exceptions under Cranman applies. Id. In this case, the parties dispute 
whether Officer Coleman's conduct is covered by a Cr anman category 
and, if a Cranman category applie s, whether Angel established an 
exception. Angel asserts that, if Officer Coleman's conduct falls under a 
Cranman category, one of the exceptio ns would apply, i.e., that he was 
acting beyond his authorit y at the time of the acci dent. Although it is 
unclear, the circuit cour t appears to have implicitly concluded that a 
Cranman category applies, because th e court explicitly concluded that 
there is substantial evidence indicati ng that an exception to immunity 
applies, i.e., that Officer Coleman exc eeded his authority by "fail[ing] to 
SC-2025-0482 
9 

follow mandatory rules and procedures by using his personal phone to 
play and listen to a YouTube video" when the accident occurred. That is, 
the circuit court evidently determined that Officer Coleman had met his 
burden and, thus, that the burden ha d shifted to Angel to show that an 
exception applies. 
II. 
Officer Coleman and the city argue that Officer Coleman's conduct 
at the time of the accident was covered under the fourth Cranman 
category, quoted above. Insofar as th e circuit court may have implicitly 
determined that Officer Coleman's conduct was covered under the fourth 
Cranman category, the circuit court was correct. As noted, under the 
fourth Cranman category, a State agen t is immune from liability in his 
or her individual capacity when the conduct underlying the claim is based 
on the State agent's "exercising ju dgment in the enforcement of the 
criminal laws of the State, including, but not limited to, law-enforcement 
officers' arresting or attempting to arrest persons[, or serving as peace 
officers under circumstances entitling such officers to immunity 
pursuant to § 6-5-338(a), Ala. Code 1975]." 792 So. 2d at 405 (the 
bracketed language is the modification added by Hollis, see 950 So. 2d at 
SC-2025-0482 
10 

309). Thus, this Court has incorpor ated the peace-officer-immunity 
standard provided in § 6-5-338(a)

leads.text:
Rel: October 16, 2026

Notice: This opinion is subject to formal revision before publication in the advance sheets of Southern
Reporter. Readers are requested to notify the Reporter of Decisions, Alabama Appellate Courts,
300 Dexter Avenue, Montgomery, Alabama 36104-3741 ((334) 229-0650), of any typographical or other
errors, in order that corrections may be made before the opinion is printed in Southern Reporter.

 SUPREME COURT OF ALABAMA
 OCTOBER TERM, 2026-2027

 _________________________

 SC-2026-0190
 _________________________

 Commercial Properties, Inc.

 v.

 Ourania Charalambidou, Dionysios Mitsios, and Montgomery
 Civic Ballet, Inc., d/b/a Montgomery Ballet Studios

 _________________________

 SC-2026-0191
 _________________________

 Ourania Charalambidou, Dionysios Mitsios, and Montgomery
 Civic Ballet, Inc., d/b/a Montgomery Ballet Studios
 SC-2026-0190 and SC-2026-0191

 v.

 Commercial Properties, Inc.

 Appeals from Montgomery Circuit Court
 (CV-21-900117)

SELLERS, Justice.

 These consolidated appeals involve two commercial leases executed

by Commercial Properties, Inc. ("the landlord"), and Montgomery Civic

Ballet, Inc., doing business as Montgomery Ballet Studios ("the Ballet").

Dionysios Mitsios ("Danny") is the executive director of the Ballet, and

Ourania Charalambidou ("Rania") is his wife. In appeal no. SC-2026-

0191, the Ballet, Danny, and Rania appeal from separate orders of the

Montgomery Circuit Court ("the trial court"), striking as untimely their

response to the landlord's motion for a partial summary judgment and

subsequently denying the resubmission of that response. We affirm. In

appeal no. SC-2026-0190, the landlord cross-appeals from the trial court's

February 3, 2026, order certifying its motion for a partial summary

judgment as final pursuant to Rule 54(b), Ala. R. Civ. P., while, at the

 2
 SC-2026-0190 and SC-2026-0191

same time, purportedly dismissing the entire case. We affirm in part,

reverse in part, and remand.

 I. Facts

 The landlord and the Ballet entered into two separate lease

agreements in May 2008 and January 2012, respectively, pursuant to

which the landlord leased to the Ballet two suites located in a shopping

center owned and managed by the landlord. The lease agreements

contained a provision for indemnification by the tenant, a default

provision, and a provision outlining when the tenant would be liable for

attorney fees and costs incurred by the landlord.1 In December 2020, the

Ballet vacated the premises based on the landlord's alleged failure to

eliminate mold that existed in the leased premises.

 In January 2021, the Ballet, Danny, and Rania filed a multicount

complaint against the landlord, alleging that Danny and Rania had

suffered personal injuries after being exposed to mold in the leased

premises. The Ballet also claimed that the mold had caused damage to

its personal property, including its costumes. The landlord answered the

 1The Ballet, Danny, and Rania do not challenge the provisions of

the lease agreements upon which the landlord relied in seeking a partial
summary judgment; therefore, we do not quote or discuss them.
 3
 SC-2026-0190 and SC-2026-0191

complaint and filed a counterclaim, seeking unpaid rent under the lease

agreements and defense and indemnity from the Ballet on the claims

asserted by Danny and Rania. The landlord thereafter sent the Ballet a

letter demanding that the Ballet defend and indemnify it on the claims

asserted by Danny and Rania, as required by the lease agreements. The

Ballet did not respond to that demand.

 In February 2023, the landlord filed a motion for a partial summary

judgment, supported by various documents. The motion for a partial

summary judgment addressed only the claims involving the Ballet, and

not Danny's and Rania's claims against the landlord. In that motion, the

landlord sought

 "(1) an interlocutory judgment declaring that [the Ballet]
 owes [the landlord] $65,827.50 in unpaid rent, the judgment
 to become a final judgment after the amount of prejudgment
 interest and fees are submitted to [the trial court]; (2) [an]
 interlocutory judgment declaring that [the] Ballet owes [the
 landlord] defense and indemnity on the claims asserted
 against it by [Danny and Rania], the claims to become a final
 judgment at the time all claims in this matter are adjudicated
 and the total amount of attorneys' fees are submitted; and (3)
 [a] final judgment against the Ballet and in favor of [the
 landlord] on [the] Ballet's claims against it. There are no
 issues as to any material fact, and [the landlord] is entitled to
 [a] judgment as a matter of law on these claims."

 4
 SC-2026-0190 and SC-2026-0191

 On March 25, 2025, the trial court entered an order setting a

hearing on the partial-summary-judgment motion for April 21, 2025, at

10:00 a.m.2 On April 18, 2025, the Ballet, Danny, and Rania filed their

response in opposition to the partial-summary-judgment motion. Before

the hearing commenced, the landlord filed a motion to strike the response

as untimely. Following the hearing, the trial court entered an order

granting the motion to strike, thus leaving the motion for a partial

summary judgment unopposed. However, the trial court did not enter an

order on the partial-summary-judgment motion -- presumably because of

an oversight.

 On October 20, 2025, the landlord moved the trial court to enter an

order on its motion for a partial summary judgment. The trial court

entered an order setting the matter for a hearing on December 3, 2025,

noting that all "pending motions" would be heard at that time. The

 2According to the landlord, the delay between the filing of the
motion for a partial summary judgment in February 2023 and the
scheduling of the hearing in March 2025 was not caused by any action or
inaction on behalf of the parties. Rather, the landlord points out that
Judge Johnny Hardwick, the original circuit-court judge assigned to hear
the matter, was assaulted while the action was pending and suffered
severe injuries that kept him from his duties. Shortly after setting the
April 21, 2025, hearing, Judge Hardwick retired, and the case was
assigned to Circuit Court Judge Tiffany McCord.
 5
 SC-2026-0190 and SC-2026-0191

Ballet, Danny, and Rania filed a "response" to the landlord's motion for

an order on the partial summary judgment, and they resubmitted the

same response that the trial court had previously deemed untimely. The

landlord filed a motion to strike the response, arguing that the trial court

had already entered an order striking it as untimely.

 On December 22, 2025, following a hearing, the trial court entered

an order denying the "renewed" response filed by the Ballet, Danny, and

Rania and entering a partial summary judgment in favor of the landlord.

The Ballet, Danny, and Rania moved the trial court to certify the partial

summary judgment in favor of the landlord as final pursuant to Rule

54(b), Ala. R. Civ. P.

 On February 3, 2026, the trial court entered an order certifying the

partial summary judgment in favor of the landlord as final pursuant to

Rule 54(b) and indicating that "this case is dismissed." This appeal and

cross-appeal followed.

 II. Standard of Review

 "This Court's review of a summary judgment is de novo.
 Williams v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 886 So. 2d 72, 74
 (Ala. 2003). We apply the same standard of review as the trial
 court applied. Specifically, we must determine whether the
 movant has made a prima facie showing that no genuine issue
 of material fact exists and that the movant is entitled to a
 6
 SC-2026-0190 and SC-2026-0191

 judgment as a matter of law. Rule 56(c), Ala. R. Civ. P.; Blue
 Cross & Blue Shield of Alabama v. Hodurski, 899 So. 2d 949,
 952-53 (Ala. 2004)."

Dow v. Alabama Democratic Party, 897 So. 2d 1035, 1038 (Ala. 2004). A

trial court's decision to strike an untimely submission offered in response

to a motion for a summary judgment is reviewed under an excess-of-

discretion standard of review. Speer v. Pin Palace Bowling Alley, 599 So.

2d 1140 (Ala. 1992).

 III. Discussion

 A. Appeal No. SC-2026-0191 -- Timeliness of Opposition

 In their appeal, the Ballet, Danny, and Rania ("the plaintiffs") do

not challenge the merits of the partial summary judgment entered in

favor of the landlord.3 Rather, they challenge only the April 21, 2025,

order striking as untimely their response to the partial summary-

judgment motion and the December 22, 2025, order denying that same

response. The plaintiffs first claim that their response was timely

 3For the first time in their reply brief, the plaintiffs attempted to

challenge the merits of the partial summary judgment. However, we will
not consider their arguments. See Lloyd Noland Hosp. v. Durham, 906
So. 2d 157, 173 (Ala. 2005) ("It is a well-established principle of appellate
review that we will not consider an issue not raised in an appellant's
initial brief, but raised only in the reply brief.").
 7
 SC-2026-0190 and SC-2026-0191

because, they say, it was filed three calendar days before the April 21,

2025, hearing. However, the plaintiffs fail to acknowledge the interplay

between Rule 56(c)(2), Ala. R. Civ. P., and Rule 6(a), Ala. R. Civ. P.,

concerning the computation of periods specified in the rules. Rule

56(c)(2) provides that a "motion for summary judgment, with all

supporting materials, including any briefs, shall be served at least ten

(10) days before the time fixed for the hearing" and that responses in

opposition to a summary-judgment motion must be served two days

before the hearing on the motion. The version of Rule 6(a) in effect at the

time the partial-summary-judgment motion was filed provided that, in

computing any period specified in the rules, "the day of the act, event, or

default from which the designated period of time begins to run shall not

be included" and that, when a filing must be accomplished within 11 days

or less, "intermediate Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays shall be

excluded in the computation." Therefore, pursuant to Rule 56(c) and Rule

6(a), the day of the hearing on the partial-summary-judgment motion

(April 21) and the Saturday and Sunday preceding the hearing (April 19

and 20) are excluded from computation; thus, any response in opposition

was due on Thursday, April 17, 2025, two business days before the

 8
 SC-2026-0190 and SC-2026-0191

hearing. See Elliott Builders, Inc. v. Timbercreek Prop. Owners Ass'n,

128 So. 3d 755, 765 (Ala. Civ. App. 2013) (indicating that Rule 56(c)(2)

"requires that matters in opposition to a summary-judgment motion

must be filed and served two days (i.e., two business days, see Rule 6(a),

Ala. R. Civ. P.) before the hearing on the motion"). Accordingly, the filing

of the response on the Friday before the scheduled hearing on Monday

was untimely.

 The plaintiffs also contend that, by striking their response in

opposition to the landlord's partial-summary-judgment motion, they

were denied the opportunity to be heard on both the partial-summary-

judgment motion and the motion to strike their response. The plaintiffs

cite Moore v. Prudential Residential Services Ltd. Partnership, 849 So.

2d 914, 926 (Ala. 2002) ("Rule 56(c)(2), Ala. R. Civ. P., gives the

nonmoving party certain rights to notice and a hearing after a summary-

judgment motion has been filed."). However, it is clear that the plaintiffs

had notice of both the April 21, 2025, hearing on the motion for a partial

summary judgment and the motion to strike that was filed and ruled

upon on that same date. To the extent that counsel for the plaintiffs failed

 9
 SC-2026-0190 and SC-2026-0191

to attend that hearing, we will not fault the trial court for that absence.4

Furthermore, although the plaintiffs assert that the requirements of

Rule 56(c)(2) are procedural in nature and that a trial court is afforded

leads.caseName: Tony Lee and Emily Boles v. Diana Sue Vest
leads.text:
Rel: October 16, 2026

Notice: This opinion is subject to formal revision before publication in the advance sheets of Southern
Reporter. Readers are requested to notify the Reporter of Decisions, Alabama Appellate Courts,
300 Dexter Avenue, Montgomery, Alabama 36104-3741 ((334) 229-0650), of any typographical or other
errors, in order that corrections may be made before the opinion is printed in Southern Reporter.

 SUPREME COURT OF ALABAMA
 OCTOBER TERM, 2026-2027

 _________________________

 SC-2026-0203
 _________________________

 Tony Lee and Emily Boles

 v.

 Diana Sue Vest

 Appeal from Talladega Circuit Court
 (CV-25-900090)

SELLERS, Justice.

 Tony Lee and his wife Emily Boles ("Lee and Boles") appeal from a

judgment of the Talladega Circuit Court ("the trial court"), ordering
 SC-2026-0203

specific performance of an option to purchase contained in a lease

agreement executed by Lee and Boles and Diana Sue Vest. We affirm

with instructions.

 I. Facts

 Lee and Boles leased to Vest a mobile home and property ("the

property") located in Lincoln for a term beginning on October 5, 2022, and

ending on June 5, 2024, for $1,500 per month. The lease agreement

contained the following option to purchase:

 "OPTION TO PURCHASE: Tenant, upon satisfactory
 performance of this Lease, shall have the option to purchase
 the real property described herein for a purchase price of
 $275,000.00 provided that the Tenant timely executes the
 option to purchase and is not in default of the Lease
 Agreement. Thereafter, each of the parties shall promptly
 execute any and all further instructions or other documents
 including a Sale Agreement which may be reasonably
 required for purchase of the real property.

 "….

 "OPTION CONSIDERATION: Non-refundable option
 consideration in the amount of $30,000.00 paid by the Tenant
 as consideration for this Option to Purchase Agreement shall
 be credited to the purchase price at closing if the Tenant
 timely exercises the option to purchase. If the Tenant doesn't
 exercise the option to purchase, the Tenant shall forfeit the
 nonrefundable option consideration."

 The lease agreement also contained a holdover clause, providing:

 2
 SC-2026-0203

 "HOLDOVER: If Tenant maintains possession of the
 Premises for any period after the termination of this Lease
 ('Holdover Period'), Tenant shall pay to Landlord lease
 payment(s) during the Holdover Period at a rate equal to
 150% of the most recent rate preceding the Holdover Period.
 Such holdover shall constitute a month-to-month extension of
 this Lease."

 Vest timely exercised her option to purchase the property and

tendered the nonrefundable option consideration of $30,000, and the

closing was scheduled for June 5, 2024, and extended until June 10, 2024.

According to Lee and Boles, Vest failed to tender the required funds to

close the sale of the property as scheduled, thus voiding the option to

purchase. Lee and Boles thereafter commenced an action against Vest,

asserting claims of breach of contract, ejectment, and unjust enrichment.

Vest responded with a counterclaim alleging breach of contract and

seeking specific performance of the option to purchase. At the request of

Lee and Boles, the trial court entered an order requiring Vest to pay

$2,000 per month into an escrow account, beginning June 2024, for the

use and occupancy of the property pending the outcome of the litigation.

See, e.g., Coan v. Championship Prop., LLC, 404 So. 3d 237 (Ala. 2024)

(noting that the trial court's escrow order was designed as an equitable

remedy to maintain the status quo and to protect the parties' competing

 3
 SC-2026-0203

interests to property, pending a final ruling on the issue of right to

possession). For their part, Lee and Boles continued paying the note on

the property, along with property taxes and homeowner's insurance,

pending a bench trial.

 The evidence presented during the bench trial was largely

undisputed. In early spring 2024, Vest exercised her option to purchase

the property and, as required by the lease agreement, tendered the

nonrefundable option consideration of $30,000 to be credited to the

purchase price of the property; the closing was scheduled for June 5,

2024, the last day of the lease term. According to Lee, he had insisted

that Luke Henderson handle the closing, and he acknowledged that

Henderson owed the same duty to Vest that he owed to Lee and Boles.

Lee and Boles did not attend the closing; rather, they signed the closing

documents a couple of weeks beforehand. Vest also intended to close

remotely, because she was scheduled to fly out of the country on the day

of the closing.

 On May 31, 2024, five days before the closing, Vest sent Henderson

an email, apparently one of several, informing him that she would be out

of town the following week and requesting that he send an accurate

 4
 SC-2026-0203

closing statement so that she could arrange for the payment to close the

transaction. Henderson responded to that email, apologizing for the

delay and stating that he would send the final closing documents later

that afternoon for her review and signature. Henderson thereafter sent

Vest an email attaching the final closing documents, reflecting an

amount due of $226,246.20 and informing her that she could wire the

funds via the instructions included in the closing package or send a

cashier's check made payable to Luke A. Henderson, LLC. On that same

date, Vest deposited $226,246.20 into her checking account.

 On June 1, 2024, Vest sent Henderson an email attaching the

signed closing documents. In that email, Vest reminded Henderson,

among other things, that she would be out of the country the following

week, that she felt Lee was trying to cancel the parties' contract, and that

she felt rushed to close on the property because she had only received the

closing documents on May 31, 2024. She therefore requested that the

closing be postponed until she returned from her trip on June 9, 2024.

 On June 4, 2026, the day before Vest left to go out of the country,

she informed Henderson that she had been unsuccessful in getting a

cashier's check for the closing because, she said, her bank either limited

 5
 SC-2026-0203

the amount of money she could wire or because the funds she had

previously deposited to purchase the property were still "pending." Vest

read the lease and noted that it did not require certified funds; she

informed Henderson that she was overnighting a personal check and

that, if he had not cashed her check by the time she returned from her

trip, she would send the certified funds to close to transaction.

 On June 5, 2024, Henderson sent Vest an email informing her that

he had received her check and that he had gone to her bank and

requested that the check be converted to a cashier's check, but that the

bank had declined his request because he was not the account holder; the

bank further advised that the check would not clear for 14 days.

Henderson also informed Vest that Lee and Boles had agreed to extend

the closing until June 10, 2024, and that to conclude the closing, she

would need either a cashier's check or a wire transfer in the amount of

$226,246.20 by the end of the business day on June 10, 2024.

 On June 8, 10, and 12, 2024, Vest sent emails to Henderson asking

whether her check had been destroyed and informing him that she felt

uncomfortable wiring additional funds until she knew the disposition of

her check. Vest received no response.

 6
 SC-2026-0203

 On June 10, 2024, after receiving no response from Henderson, Lee,

or Boles for two days, Vest stopped payment on her check. On that same

date, Vest sent an email to Lee stating that she had not heard from him

and that Henderson had never responded to her email about the

whereabouts of her check. Vest further indicated that, because

Henderson was no longer communicating with her, she needed to know

how to proceed with closing the transaction.

 On June 11, 2024, without Vest's authorization or consent, Lee

went to Henderson's office and demanded that he indorse Vest's check

over to him so that he could deposit it into his account. When questioned

by Vest's attorney, Lee candidly testified:

 "Q. All right. Anyway, you changed your mind [about the
 personal check] and you went to [Henderson's] office, didn't
 you?

 "A. I did.

 "Q. Okay. And you went down there and you instructed that
 attorney to endorse that check over to you and -- so you could
 deposit it in the bank; correct?

 "A. Correct.

 "Q. Okay. And tell me by what authority do you have to go to
 the attorney and instruct him to endorse that check when he
 owes her the same duty that he owes you?

 7
 SC-2026-0203

 "A. Well, it was the check meant to pay for the house that
 she's living in that belongs to me, so the check was coming to
 us anyhow, so --

 "Q. What do you mean --

 "A. -- it was my money.

 "….

 "Q. So if certified funds were required, then why are you
 changing your mind to deposit a personal check that you said
 could not be used to consummate a real estate closing
 transaction? You testified to that previously, didn't you?

 "A. Yeah.

 "Q. Well, then, why were you getting her personal check and
 putting it in the bank?

 "A. Well, we needed the money. I mean --

 "Q. You needed the money, but you said a personal check
 could not be used on a conveyance of property. Those are your
 words. I guess they were going to be if you were going to put
 it in the bank, the personal check; correct?

 "A. Yeah."

According to Lee, Henderson also gave him the entire closing file.

 On June 12, 2024, Vest informed Lee about the stop-payment order,

adding that she was uncomfortable with Henderson's "sitting on her

check" because he had been unresponsive. Vest further expressed her

willingness to wire the funds directly to Lee and Boles if acceptable. On
 8
 SC-2026-0203

that same date, Boles responded to that email, informing Vest that,

because she had stopped payment on the check, the location of her check

was irrelevant and had no bearing on her ability to wire the certified

funds. Nonetheless, Boles informed Vest that Henderson had indorsed

the check over to her and Lee for deposit. In that same email, Boles also

informed Vest that she and Lee were in the process of taking legal steps

to secure the property and that if Vest wanted to bring everything to a

closure, she could simply wire the funds to their personal account the

following day by 10:00 a.m. Although Vest expressed in one of her emails

a willingness to wire the certified funds directly to Lee and Boles, she

nonetheless testified that she did not feel comfortable doing so without

an attorney being involved.1 Lee and Boles thereafter sent Vest a letter

informing her that the option to purchase had expired and that the lease

would not be renewed. Notably, Boles testified in her deposition that,

after she and Lee commenced this action, they continued to discuss

closing the real-estate transaction with Vest because, according to Boles,

they were desperate to do so.

 1Some of the emails referenced herein were sent by Dennis
Flannagan, on Vest's behalf. It appears that Dennis was Vest's friend
and/or roommate.
 9
 SC-2026-0203

 At the conclusion of bench trial, the trial court expressed its opinion

that the closing would have occurred but for the conduct of Henderson

and Lee and Boles. The trial court asked Vest if she remained ready,

willing, and able to close the real-estate transaction, to which she

responded "yes." At that point, the trial court asked counsel for the

parties whether they could agree to a closing date if the court ordered

specific performance and, if so, whether they could provide certain

documentation allowing the trial court to make necessary calculations.

The parties agreed to a closing date and provided the trial court with the

requested do
